INTRODUCTION

What this Teacher's Book is and how it was built

This volume exists so that a competent English teacher can prepare and deliver any lesson in Grammar for Special Speaking without having to invent missing explanations, answers, procedures or activities.

Every guide that follows corresponds, line by line, to the Student Book: the same sixteen lessons in the same order, the same eight lesson functions, the same practice items and the same answer key. The teaching content in this book and the practice content in the Student Book are generated from a single shared source, so the two volumes cannot drift apart between editions.

Each guide gives you: measurable lesson outcomes and success criteria; materials and preparation; a sixty-minute timing plan that matches the Student Book's pacing guidance; step-by-step procedures for all eight lesson functions; quick checks for understanding; the complete practice answers with notes on where learners lose marks; model exchanges and model responses for the speaking tasks; assessment guidance for open-ended work; Intermediate scaffolding and Advanced extension; common learner errors with correction strategies; a forty-five-minute shorter-session plan; and review and feedback guidance.

The Student Book's assessment policy carries over unchanged: model answers are examples, not scripts; acceptable alternatives are accepted wherever an exercise allows them; speaking tasks are judged with success criteria and the four-criterion rubric, not with a single mandatory response; and the Diagnostic Test and Final Assessment raw totals must not be compared as a measure of learning gain.

What this book does not claim: it is not a record of classroom trials, teacher certification, or external approval. Its procedures are editorially prepared and structurally verified; qualified-teacher review and a real learner pilot remain separate, documented steps.

Assessment architecture

• Diagnostic Test (25 written items + matched baseline speaking sample) — before Lesson 1.

• Review Test 1 after Lesson 4 (scope: Lessons 1–4); Review Test 2 after Lesson 8 (1–8); Review Test 3 after Lesson 12 (1–12). Cumulative, taught material only.

• Final Assessment after Lesson 16: 30 written items with an item-level coverage matrix, plus the matched speaking task and four-criterion rubric.

• Five appendices in the Student Book: Formula Book, Common Errors Guide, Sentence Patterns, Can-Do Tracker and the Complete Answer Key (Appendix 5).

TEACHING PRINCIPLES

The instructional philosophy behind every guide

Meaning first, form second.

Every lesson opens with the Speaking Hook: learners speak before they see the rule, so the grammar arrives as a tool they were already reaching for.

Keep explanation short, production long.

The Simple Rule and See the Difference should take a quarter of the lesson at most; the remaining time belongs to guided and spoken use.

Accuracy and fluency alternate.

Controlled practice builds accuracy; Pair Speaking rehearses with support; the Real Talk Challenge demands independent transfer. Do not collapse the three into one.

Correction that protects speaking.

Do not interrupt fluency work to fix errors. Note them, finish the task, then repair together — see the Pacing and Feedback section.

Models are examples, never scripts.

Printed models illustrate effective language. Learners produce their own versions; accept any response that meets the success criteria.

One objective, two pathways.

Intermediate learners secure the core pattern with scaffolds; Advanced learners deepen choice, register and precision. Advanced work must add precision, not merely workload.

Assessment stays honest.

Accept legitimate alternatives, assess speaking with criteria rather than a single answer, and never present raw diagnostic and final totals as a gain score.

Return-to-rule on failure.

When a self-check box is unticked, the learner goes back to the Simple Rule, redoes the matching practice item, and revisits the Formula Book card before moving on.

Session variants

• 45-minute lesson: follow the shorter-session box printed in each guide — the core objective, controlled practice and a shortened supported speaking task survive; the Advanced upgrade moves to independent study.

• 90-minute lesson: run the full guide, then repeat the Real Talk Challenge with a new partner and finish with the Review and Self-Check written twice (second attempt in different words).

• Multiple weekly sessions: place a review-test day between lesson blocks rather than compressing two lessons into one hour.

Feedback that protects fluency

During speaking tasks — do not interrupt

• Listen with the printed success criteria; tick what you hear instead of writing while learners speak.

• Note one or two recurring global errors (tense choice, word order) on the board anonymously — never one note per learner.

• Praise one specific success per speaker: a structure, a repair, a follow-up question.

After the task — repair in three minutes

• Recast once, ask the class to rebuild the sentence, then say the model version.

• Correct only what was taught in this lesson; file other errors for a later review.

• Send learners back to the printed Watch out list in Part 8 for self-correction before you supply answers.

• With Advanced learners, ask them to justify their choice of structure — discussion is correction too.

LESSON 1 · TENSES FOR REAL COMMUNICATION — TEACHER GUIDE

Part 1 — Build Strong Sentences | Speaking goal: talk about habits, experiences and changes accurately

This guide mirrors the Student Book lesson exactly: the same eight functions, the same practice items and the same answers. Follow the parts in order; adapt the timing to your class.

Lesson outcomes and measurable success criteria

By the end of the lesson

• Choose accurate forms for habits, current situations, finished past events and future arrangements in spoken sentences.

• Explain in one sentence why a finished-time expression takes the past simple rather than the present perfect.

• Deliver a one-minute account of their English improvement using at least three different tense families with correct time expressions.

Success criteria — the learner can:

✓ at least 4 of 5 Practice A items correct before the key is displayed

✓ corrections in Practice B are justified with a time reason, not a guess

✓ in the Real Talk Challenge, time expressions match the chosen tense every time

Materials and preparation

Before the lesson

• Board with three columns: NOW (present tenses) · FINISHED (past simple) · CONNECTED TO NOW (present perfect) · NEXT (future choices).

• No photocopies required; learners write only keywords during planning.

• Optional: phone or recorder for one Real Talk attempt to replay in the next lesson.

Suggested timing (60-minute lesson)

Lesson part

Minutes

The Speaking Hook

5

The Simple Rule

7

See the Difference

3

Practice the Pattern

10

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

• Display the four hook questions. Learners answer all four in pairs — books closed; the point is to hear which tenses they already reach for.

• Take two contrasting samples whole-class ('What has changed since last year?') and underline the time words learners used.

• Tell learners the lesson will give them precise choices for exactly these answers.

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

• Teach the three rule groups in order: present tenses, past simple vs present perfect, future choices. One formula box, two or three examples each — nothing more.

• Read each Examples line aloud and have the class repeat one sentence per group.

• Contrast 'I saw him yesterday' with 'I have seen him recently' on the board to fix the finished-time rule with its 'recently' qualification.

Check understanding — quick, whole-class

• 'Last year I…' — which tense? (past simple) · 'Since 2021 she has…' — why not 'worked'?

• Fast fingers: show a time phrase card; learners point to the NOW, FINISHED, CONNECTED or NEXT column.

• Ask two learners to give opposite answers with the same verb: 'I work here' vs 'I'm working here this month.'

Part 3 · See the Difference

• Cover the right-hand column of the first table and ask pairs to predict the difference before revealing it.

• Drill the state-verb line: learners correct 'I am knowing' chorally, then produce their own state-verb sentence.

• Ask: 'Which time words force the past simple?' — expect: yesterday, last…, in 2020, when…

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

• Set Practice A (5 items) — 3 minutes alone, then compare in pairs before taking whole-class answers.

• Set Practice B (4 tasks) — corrections must be given with a one-clause reason.

• Display the key only after pair checking; ask 'Why?' for any item where half the room disagrees.

Answer key — Practice A and B (identical to the Student Book key)

Practice A. 1 saw · 2 has worked / has been working · 3 are meeting · 4 is snowing · 5 believes

Practice B. 1 I finished my homework last night. · 2 She knows the answer. · 3 have you known · 4 I'm going to study medicine.

Where learners lose marks — teaching notes

• A1 'saw' — 'last week' is a finished time; any present perfect here is an error, not a variant.

• A2 accepts 'has worked / has been working' — since 2022 keeps the situation open, so both aspects are correct; the continuous adds emphasis on continuation.

• A3 'are meeting' — an arrangement with a time word takes the present continuous for the future; 'will meet' loses the arrangement meaning.

• B3 'have you known' — 'How long' asks about a period continuing to now; 'do you know' asks about present knowledge and is possible only with a different reading, which this item rules out.

• B4 'I'm going to study medicine' — a decided plan; a bare 'I will study' would signal a decision made while speaking.

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

• Model one interview round with a confident learner first: ask, listen, ask a follow-up — then hand over to pairs.

• Run the four questions; circulate with the success criteria and tick evidence.

• Close with two samples: one learner reports what their partner said (past + present perfect mix).

Model exchange for rehearsal (one possible version)

A: What do you usually do at the weekend? B: I usually visit my family, and on Sunday I play football. — A: Nice. How long have you been playing? B: Since school. What did you do last night? A: I studied for two hours, then I watched a film. B: What has changed in your life since last year? A: I speak English at work now — I got a new job in March.

Part 6 · The Advanced Upgrade

• Intermediate base: pairs check the time-cue drill aloud; each makes three true sentences (habit, current project, recent experience).

• Advanced upgrade: pairs produce the present-perfect continuous sentence and the 'It's the first time I've…' emphasis frame, then explain when each is better than the simple forms.

• Ask one pair to defend a choice: 'Why present perfect, not past simple?'

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

• Give the planning time exactly as printed (30 seconds, keywords only) — no full sentences on paper.

• First attempt to a partner (1 minute). Model response stays covered.

• Uncover the model; learners underline its tense choices, then retell their own content with one improved structure.

Model response (as printed in the Student Book)

I've been studying English seriously for about two years. Last year I joined a speaking club, and that was the moment things changed — I learned to think in English instead of translating every sentence. These days I listen to a short podcast every morning, and I'm still working on my pronunciation. My grammar is much better than it was, but speaking fluently is what I'm focusing on now.

Assessing this open-ended task

• Use the four printed feedback bullets as live criteria; tick what you hear, do not write during the two minutes.

• The model is one strong version — accept any response that names a past event, explains the learning, and states current work with matching time words.

• Score nothing here; note two learners who confused finished and open time for a three-minute repair at the end.

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

• Run the retrieval prompts orally — cover the page first, as printed.

• Collect the two 'Watch out' corrections as a whole-class chorus.

• Learners tick the self-check boxes; anyone with an unticked box returns to the Simple Rule and a Practice A item before the next lesson.

Differentiation: Intermediate and Advanced pathways

Intermediate — scaffolding and remediation

• Give a cue card set: yesterday / since 2021 / tomorrow 10 a.m. / these days — learners match each to a tense before speaking.

• Sentence starters: 'I have been… since…' · 'Last year I…' · 'I'm going to…'

• Remediation: if A1/A2 were wrong, re-do those two items orally with new time words before the pair task; delay the Real Talk Challenge until the correction lands.

Advanced — extension and discussion guidance

• Discussion: 'Which sounds more natural — I've seen her recently or I saw her recently? When would you choose each?' Expect the time-focus answer.

• Upgrade task: combine past simple and present perfect in one sentence about a real failure and its lesson.

• Extension: learners write one 'It's the first time I've…' sentence about an experience they actually had, then say it with stress on the experience.

Common learner errors and targeted correction

Expect these — and fix them like this

• 'I have seen him yesterday.' → 'I saw him yesterday.' — fix: ask 'Is the time finished?' before choosing a tense; run a 60-second drill with four time phrases.

• 'She is knowing the answer.' → 'She knows the answer.' — fix: list state verbs on the board (know, believe, own, seem) and sort five verbs into state/action.

• 'We will meet tomorrow at ten' for a fixed arrangement — fix: contrast 'I'll help you' (decision now) with 'we're meeting at ten' (arrangement) using the learners' own timetables.

Shorter-session adaptation (45 minutes)

Keep the objective, cut the load

• Keep Parts 1–4 at 15 + 10 exactly; drop the second pair sample.

• Pair Speaking: run questions 1 and 4 only (habit + change), still with follow-ups.

• Real Talk Challenge: 45 seconds of speech, 15 seconds planning; move the model comparison into the self-check at the end.

Review, consolidation and feedback

Close the loop

• Use the two retrieval prompts as the exit ticket for the lesson.

• Record 'has worked / has been working' as a standing acceptable-alternative reminder for future marking.

• Next lesson's warm-up: one past-simple sentence about yesterday from every learner.

Feedback for this lesson's speaking

Tick tense/time matches during the pair interview rather than interrupting; afterwards, put three anonymous sentences on the board — one good, two faulty — and let the class repair them before you confirm.

LESSON 2 · TELLING STORIES AND DESCRIBING EXPERIENCES — TEACHER GUIDE

Part 1 — Build Strong Sentences | Speaking goal: tell a story with background, sequence and clear focus

This guide mirrors the Student Book lesson exactly: the same eight functions, the same practice items and the same answers. Follow the parts in order; adapt the timing to your class.

Lesson outcomes and measurable success criteria

By the end of the lesson

• Tell a short story that separates background (past continuous), events (past simple) and the earlier past (past perfect).

• Use at least three sequence markers correctly in a two-minute narrative.

• Retell a partner's story in three sentences without losing its order.

Success criteria — the learner can:

✓ the spoken story contains one accurate background scene and one past perfect clause

✓ the listener can repeat the events in the correct order

✓ at least three sequence words appear (first, then, by the time, suddenly, finally)

Materials and preparation

Before the lesson

• Board story shape: BACKGROUND → EVENTS → EARLIER → ENDING.

• Optional: two short anecdote openings written on slips for weaker pairs.

• Timer visible to learners for the ten-second plan in the Real Talk Challenge.

Suggested timing (60-minute lesson)

Lesson part

Minutes

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

• Give every learner 30 seconds to tell a short story to their partner — no planning time, no notes.

• Listeners name the moment that felt most important and why (funny, surprising, sudden).

• Collect two whole-class examples and mark the shape they used on the board.

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

• Teach the three levels as one system: background, events, earlier past. Use the Examples lines as choral reading.

• Board drill: 'While I was walking… when I met… because I had forgotten…' — learners fill each slot with their own content.

• Mark 'when + past simple' and 'while + past continuous' as a fixed pair, then read the 'by the time' remember line.

Check understanding — quick, whole-class

• 'While I was walking' vs 'When I walked' — which takes the -ing form? (while)

• Show 'By the time we arrived, the film had started.' — learners identify the two past moments and point to the earlier one.

• Quick transform: 'She studied. The lights went out.' → learners say the background version aloud.

Part 3 · See the Difference

• Use the three-column table as a substitution drill: same sentence, three levels — learners transform 'He took a taxi' across the row.

• Ask which level answers 'what was already happening?' — expect past continuous.

• Story-shape recap: one learner narrates the printed example scene end to end.

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

• Practice A (6 items) solo (4 minutes), then同伴 check — emphasise A5/A6 agreement of tenses across two clauses.

• Practice B (6 tasks): pairs transform first, whole class confirms; B3 and B4 are spoken, not written.

• Display the key; drill aloud any item where the past perfect was omitted.

Answer key — Practice A and B (identical to the Student Book key)

Practice A. 1 was studying · 2 had already eaten · 3 called / took · 4 was walking / saw · 5 had finished · 6 were playing / was resting

Practice B. 1 While I was reading the report, the printer broke. · 2 By the time we reached the station, the train had left. · 3 When I arrived, he had already left. · 4 answers vary · 5 while · 6 It was raining and I forgot my umbrella, so I got wet. (answers vary)

Where learners lose marks — teaching notes

• A5 'had finished' — 'By 2019' sets a past deadline; the action is earlier than a past reference point.

• A6 tests agreement: 'were playing / was resting' — the second clause may be past continuous or past simple; both are accepted in the key where listed.

• B3 'When I arrived, he had already left.' — the classic order fix; accept the version with 'already' moved after 'had'.

• B5 'while' — 'when' would be wrong here because the phone rang inside an ongoing bath; actually accept 'when I was having a bath' only if the learner restructures the clause — explain the difference live.

• B6 is open — credit any version with a background + event + wet outcome; do not grade creativity.

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

• Set the two-minute story with the three required elements displayed as a checklist.

• Circulate and note one strength and one missing element per speaker.

• Listeners give two follow-up questions before roles swap.

Model exchange for rehearsal (one possible version)

A: Last winter I was driving to Mazar when the snow started. B: Was the road open? A: Yes, but by the time we reached the tunnel, traffic had stopped for an hour. We waited, drank tea from a thermos, and finally turned back. B: What did you do then? A: We stayed in a guesthouse — it became the best part of the trip.

Part 6 · The Advanced Upgrade

• Intermediate base: the three-level drill and the 30-second one-while/one-when/one-by-the-time story.

• Advanced upgrade: repeated-past 'would', earlier background 'had been doing', and a present reflection ending — each learner produces one of the three.

• Discussion: why is 'It taught me a lesson I've never forgotten' a strong ending?

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

• Ten seconds of silent planning only, as printed — nothing written.

• Tell partner 1, then immediately retell to partner 2: 'Tell it again, better.'

• Uncover the model; compare the model's shape (background → events → earlier → reflection) with learners' own.

Model response (as printed in the Student Book)

It was a Friday in May. I was walking home from the market when I realised I had left my phone at home — I had only been walking for ten minutes, so I turned back at once. First I checked the path behind me; then I hurried home. By the time I reached the flat, my sister had already answered a call from my cousin: he had won two tickets to the final and needed my answer straight away. I called him back immediately, and we went that night. I've checked my pockets before leaving the house ever since.

Assessing this open-ended task

• Checklist listening: background present? order logical? past perfect for the earlier action? ending explains why it mattered?

• Accept any story that meets the four criteria; do not require every target structure in every story.

• If a learner's story lacks the earlier past, prompt once after the retell: 'What had already happened?' and listen for the repair.

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

• Cover and run the two retrieval prompts — the story with one 'while' and one 'by the time' is the must-pass item.

• Self-check boxes, then a show of hands: who missed the past perfect in practice?

• Anyone unticked redoes B2 ('By the time we reached the station…') aloud.

Differentiation: Intermediate and Advanced pathways

Intermediate — scaffolding and remediation

• Provide the board shape (BACKGROUND → EVENTS → EARLIER → ENDING) as a visible scaffold during pair work.

• Offer sequence starters: First… / Then… / Suddenly… / By the time… / Finally…

• Remediation: learners who omitted past perfect re-tell a 30-second version using one 'had + participle' clause before the Real Talk Challenge.

Advanced — extension and discussion guidance

• Discuss: when does 'would + verb' sound nostalgic rather than merely repeated? (habit narratives)

• Upgrade: produce a 'had been waiting an hour when…' sentence about a real delay.

• Peer challenge: listeners award one point per correctly used level (background/events/earlier) — highest total wins.

Common learner errors and targeted correction

Expect these — and fix them like this

• 'When I arrived, he left.' for the earlier action → 'When I arrived, he had left.' — fix: timeline on the board with two past points; learners place the earlier event.

• 'While I was walking, I had seen a friend.' → 'I saw' — fix: while marks the scene, not the earlier past; re-sort four sentences into while/when/by the time.

• Sequences without connectors ('…then…then…') — fix: require one connector per event in the next retell.

Shorter-session adaptation (45 minutes)

Keep the objective, cut the load

• Parts 1–4 fixed at 15 + 10; pair stories limited to 90 seconds with one follow-up.

• Advanced upgrade becomes the homework sentence set.

• Real Talk Challenge: tell once only; the 'better second telling' moves to the next lesson's warm-up.

Review, consolidation and feedback

Close the loop

• Exit ticket: one sentence containing both 'while' and 'by the time'.

• Keep the story-shape board for Lesson 16's integrated story round.

• If past perfect is shaky class-wide, reopen Formula Book card 2 at the next session.

Feedback for this lesson's speaking

After each two-minute story, listeners retell it in three sentences — the retell itself is feedback on clarity; add your structural note only then, and always for the class, never for one speaker.

LESSON 3 · QUESTIONS, AUXILIARY VERBS, AND FOLLOW-UP QUESTIONS — TEACHER GUIDE

Part 2 — Express Ideas Clearly | Speaking goal: ask clear questions and keep a conversation alive

This guide mirrors the Student Book lesson exactly: the same eight functions, the same practice items and the same answers. Follow the parts in order; adapt the timing to your class.

Lesson outcomes and measurable success criteria

By the end of the lesson

• Form direct and indirect (polite) questions with correct word order.

• Sustain a three-minute interview using content-based follow-up questions.

• Distinguish subject questions from object questions when speaking.

Success criteria — the learner can:

✓ no inverted-word-order errors across six spoken questions

✓ at least three follow-ups react to the content of an answer, not just the topic

✓ one indirect question used naturally in the pair task

Materials and preparation

Before the lesson

• Board: question frame (Aux + subject + verb) and embedded frame (question word + subject + verb).

• Optional: soft-openers strip for weaker learners (Could you tell me… / Do you know…).

• Two-column board section for direct vs indirect examples.

9

Real Talk Challenge

10

Review and Self-Check

5

Total

60

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

• Round one: learners find out three things about their partner under the follow-up rule — one follow-up after every answer.

• Stop the class halfway and praise one genuine content follow-up you heard.

• Ask: 'Who kept the conversation alive? How?' — expect: questions about details.

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

• Teach Rule 1 with the formula boxes; drill 'Do you live here? / Where do you live?' as a pair.

• Flag the subject-question exception with 'Who called you?' — contrast 'Who did you call?' on the board.

• Rule 2 (indirect): build one together: 'Where is the bank?' → 'Could you tell me where the bank is?' and mark the no-inversion point.

• Rule 3: read the follow-up stems aloud; learners repeat all six.

Check understanding — quick, whole-class

• Thumbs: 'Do you know where is the bank?' correct? (no — thumbs down, then rebuild it).

• Fast transform: teacher says a direct question; pairs say the indirect version.

• 'Who called you?' — is there an auxiliary? Why not? (who is the subject)

Part 3 · See the Difference

• Side-by-side table drill: say the direct form, pairs produce the indirect form before reading the column.

• Board race: two teams transform 'What time does it open?' and 'Why are you late?' — fastest correct word order wins.

• Subject vs object: learners sort 'Who broke the window?' vs 'Who did you call?' into the right pattern.

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

• Practice A (6 items) — pairs first, then whole-class keys; insist on full question forms spoken aloud.

• Practice B (6 tasks): B4 follow-ups and B6 are spoken demonstrations, not written answers.

• Key display after pair check; drill any item with missing inversion.

Answer key — Practice A and B (identical to the Student Book key)

Practice A. 1 have / tried · 2 happened · 3 the library is · 4 costs · 5 wrote · 6 did / write

Practice B. 1 Could you tell me where you parked? · 2 Do you know when the results will be ready? · 3 Do you know where the bank is? · 4 answers vary · 5 Did she call you? · 6 answers vary

Where learners lose marks — teaching notes

• A3 'the library is' — embedded statement order is the whole point; any inversion here is the target error.

• A5 'wrote' vs A6 'did / write' — the pair exists to prove subject vs object questions differ; walk the pair on the board every time.

• B1/B2 accept any correct soft opener with proper embedded order — the opener may vary (Could you tell me / Do you know / I was wondering).

• B4 is open: credit two genuine content follow-ups (about what was said), not two topic switches.

• B6 open: any 'How long…' question with correct indirect or direct order as asked.

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

• Assign A/B roles, run three minutes, swap. Monitor for follow-ups with a tally on the board.

• Replay one strong exchange for the class (heard during monitoring).

• Summarise: what did you learn about your partner? One sentence each.

Model exchange for rehearsal (one possible version)

A: Do you know how you usually spend your weekends? B: I usually study in the morning and visit family in the evening. How about you? A: I play football on Fridays. B: Really — how long have you been playing? A: Since school. B: What was the proudest moment you've had this year? A: Passing my driving test. B: That's great. What are you going to do to celebrate it?

Part 6 · The Advanced Upgrade

• Intermediate base: two orders drilled plus five soft openers shadow-read.

• Advanced upgrade: negative questions for surprise, echo questions, and two question tags — each learner uses one in a real exchange.

• Discussion: when does a negative question sound suspicious rather than interested?

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

• Run exactly as printed: partner gives one starter sentence; conversation must last two minutes on questions and short reactions.

• Coach B to open with a content follow-up within two seconds of the starter.

• Compare with the model dialogue: underline its indirect question and reactions, then note one line from learners' own conversation that was better.

Model response (as printed in the Student Book)

A: I almost missed my flight last week.
B: Really? What happened next?
A: The traffic was terrible — I reached the gate twenty minutes before take-off. Do you often fly, or was this a one-off?
B: I fly for work sometimes. What's the worst journey you've ever had?
A: A train was cancelled once, so I waited six hours at the station. Have you ever missed a connection?
B: No, but I came close in Dubai. How did you get through the wait in the end?

Assessing this open-ended task

• Tally board: follow-ups heard per pair — the printed criteria (order, content follow-up, flow, equal talk) decide success, not accent or speed.

• If the conversation stalls twice, the listener may use a printed stem — that is still success for Intermediate; Advanced should manage without stems.

• No numeric score; record who needs the word-order repair drill for the next lesson.

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

• Cover and perform: one direct + one indirect question about the same thing.

• Whole-class chorus of three follow-up stems.

• Self-check; unticked boxes return to Rule 2 and B3 for correction.

Differentiation: Intermediate and Advanced pathways

Intermediate — scaffolding and remediation

• Allow the soft-opener strip during the interview; fade it in the second round.

• Sentence starters: 'What happened next?' · 'How did that feel?' · 'How about you?'

• Remediation: if embedded order slips, re-run B3 orally with three different question words before the Real Talk Challenge.

Advanced — extension and discussion guidance

• Discussion: 'Haven't you finished?' — what does the speaker assume? Contrast with 'Have you finished?'

• Upgrade: add one question tag to a statement about the partner's answer and check the auxiliary aloud.

• Precision drill: rewrite one blunt question in three polite registers for a professor, a colleague, a friend.

Common learner errors and targeted correction

Expect these — and fix them like this

• 'Do you know where is the bank?' → '…where the bank is?' — fix: draw the embedded frame and rebuild three questions with question-word cards.

• 'Did she called you?' → 'Did she call you?' — fix: after do/did, base verb only; rapid-fire five verbs after 'did'.

• Follow-ups that switch topic ('Nice. Do you like pizza?') — fix: require 'What… about X?' referring to the answer's content; model one recast.

Shorter-session adaptation (45 minutes)

Keep the objective, cut the load

• Parts 1–4 at 15 + 10; pair interview runs two topics instead of three.

• Advanced upgrade (echo/negative/tags) becomes the optional finishers' task.

• Real Talk Challenge: 90 seconds of conversation, keeping the starter-sentence format.

Review, consolidation and feedback

Close the loop

• Exit ticket: each learner asks one indirect question to the teacher before leaving.

• Collect nothing; the pairs' spoken accuracy is the data.

• Carry three follow-up stems into Lesson 4's negotiation warm-up.

Feedback for this lesson's speaking

Praise the follow-up that showed listening ('You asked about the interview, not just the topic') — name the behaviour you want; correct word order after the round, using two anonymous examples.

LESSON 4 · MODAL VERBS FOR REAL-LIFE SITUATIONS — TEACHER GUIDE

Part 2 — Express Ideas Clearly | Speaking goal: express ability, advice, obligation, permission, possibility and certainty at the right strength

This guide mirrors the Student Book lesson exactly: the same eight functions, the same practice items and the same answers. Follow the parts in order; adapt the timing to your class.

Lesson outcomes and measurable success criteria

By the end of the lesson

• Select modals by meaning — ability, advice, obligation, permission, possibility — at the right strength.

• Distinguish deduction (can't be) from prohibition (mustn't) in speech.

• Handle a polite role-play request or complaint using soft modal forms.

Success criteria — the learner can:

✓ modals in the role-play match intended strength in at least 5 of 6 cases

✓ two polite request forms used without prompting

✓ one correct deduction about visible evidence (must be / might be / can't be)

Materials and preparation

Before the lesson

• Board meanings map: ability · advice · obligation · permission · possibility · certainty.

• Role cards optional: delayed order · bad hotel room · missed class.

• Note deduction clues on the board (car gone, light on, bag packed) for Rule 2.

Suggested timing (60-minute lesson)

Lesson part

Minutes

The Speaking Hook

4

The Simple Rule

8

See the Difference

3

Practice the Pattern

10

Pair Speaking

12

The Advanced Upgrade

8

Real Talk Challenge

10

Review and Self-Check

5

Total

60

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

• Run the two hook situations as a quick pair warm-up: advice for 'My English is not improving', then the early-leave request.

• Take two responses whole-class and place each on the meanings map.

• Tell learners today's job: choosing strength, not just meaning.

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

• Rule 1: read the formula line; drill 'no -s, no to' with three wrong forms first (he cans / he can to swim) so learners hear the error.

• Rule 2: build the deduction ladder from visible evidence in the room ('The door is closed — she must be out').

• Rule 3: model two polite requests; pairs shadow both, then create one.

Check understanding — quick, whole-class

• 'You mustn't tell anyone' — meaning? (forbidden) vs 'You can't be serious' — meaning? (deduction)

• Show an action: learners fire three advice modals at it (should / could / might).

• One wrong form on the board ('He cans swim') — whole-class repair.

Part 3 · See the Difference

• Table 1 as a sorting chant: strong advice / external rule / gentle advice — teacher reads sentences, class holds up 1/2/3 fingers.

• Board the can't vs mustn't contrast in big letters with one example each; ask for a new pair from learners.

• Could vs was able to: quick oral check — general ability vs one past achievement.

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

• Practice A (6) solo then pairs; A3/A4 (certainty vs prohibition) need spoken justification.

• Practice B (6): pairs perform B1 and B5 aloud as mini-dialogues.

• Key after checking; on any confusion between mustn't and can't, stop and rebuild Rule 2 before continuing.

Answer key — Practice A and B (identical to the Student Book key)

Practice A. 1 should · 2 could · 3 must · 4 mustn't · 5 might · 6 Would / opening

Practice B. 1 Could you open the window, please? / Would you mind opening the window? · 2 She must be at home. · 3 He might have missed the train. / He may have missed the train. · 4 He can't be at home — his lights are off. · 5 No, not at all. (No problem.) · 6 answers vary

Where learners lose marks — teaching notes

• A4 'mustn't' — prohibition is the only reading for 'touch the wires'; 'can't' would mean inability or deduction and fails the context.

• A5 accepts 'might / could / may' — 50% possibility; 'must' would overstate the evidence.

• B3 accepts 'might have missed / may have missed' — past possibility; 'must have missed' is wrong (too certain) unless learners justify new evidence.

• B4: the fix changes deduction to 'can't be' — learners must state why (lights off = evidence, not rule).

• B5 'No, not at all' — teach the counter-intuitive answer to 'Would you mind…?' explicitly every time.

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

• Negotiation task: give a two-minute thinking window for the budget choice; monitor for polite forms with a tally.

• Require an announced decision: 'Our team has decided… because…'

• Two pairs perform; class listens for strength choices only.

Model exchange for rehearsal (one possible version)

A: We should choose the training course — the team needs it more than the weekend trip. B: We mustn't forget the budget, though. A: True, but we could cut the trip cost instead. B: Then you could offer to run the training yourselves — that saves the trainer's fee. A: Deal, I'll have the materials prepared by Friday. B: And the manager might approve the extra day if we show him the plan.

Part 6 · The Advanced Upgrade

• Intermediate base: job-based sorting of modals and the three deductions drill.

• Advanced upgrade: 'must have + participle' past deduction, 'would' preference, and diplomatic hedged obligation — one true sentence each.

• Discussion: why is 'We ought to reconsider' safer than 'We must change this' with a manager?

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

• Role cards out; one minute per role as printed; teacher joins a pair if numbers are odd.

• Model response uncovered only after both roles are played once.

• Underline the model's strength ladder (wondering → could → must be → should), then run a second round with one upgraded form per speaker.

Model response (as printed in the Student Book)

Client: Good morning — I was wondering if I could talk about my order. It was due on Tuesday, and it still hasn't arrived.
Professional: I'm sorry about that. You must be frustrated. Let me check… It looks like the parcel was sent to the wrong depot.
Client: In that case, could I have it redelivered tomorrow? I have to be at work, so it might need to come after five.
Professional: That should be possible. We could offer an evening slot, or I could ask the depot to hold it for collection. Which would you prefer?

Assessing this open-ended task

• Live tally against the four criteria; the decision must be reached and explained or the task is incomplete.

• Accept any modal set that shows correct strength; politeness is judged by form, not by volume or accent.

• If deduction language is absent, prompt once with a board clue ('His car is here…') during the feedback phase.

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

• Three deductions about the room, spoken chorally: must be / might be / can't be.

• Two very polite requests from different learners.

• Self-check; unticked boxes redo A4 and B4 orally.

Differentiation: Intermediate and Advanced pathways

Intermediate — scaffolding and remediation

• Meaning map stays visible during pair work; learners point before they speak.

• Frames: 'You should…' · 'Could I possibly…?' · 'She must be…'

• Remediation: if mustn't/can't keeps flipping, run the two-column correction drill from the errors box before Real Talk.

Advanced — extension and discussion guidance

• Discussion: compare 'You must see this film' (speaker enthusiasm) with 'You have to see a film' (external rule) — where is the force coming from?

• Upgrade: report a past deduction about a friend ('You must have been exhausted').

• Precision: rewrite a direct order for a client at three politeness levels.

Common learner errors and targeted correction

Expect these — and fix them like this

• 'He mustn't be at home' for deduction → 'He can't be at home' — fix: evidence vs rule drill with three pictures.

• 'Would you mind to open…?' → '…opening…' — fix: mind + -ing chorus with five verbs.

• 'He cans swim' / 'he can to swim' → 'he can swim' — fix: modal + base verb flash practice.

Shorter-session adaptation (45 minutes)

Keep the objective, cut the load

• Parts 1–4 at 15 + 10; negotiation scenario runs one option, not a three-way choice.

• Real Talk: first role only in class; second role becomes a written dialogue for homework.

• Upgrade sentences move to the self-check as spoken homework.

Review, consolidation and feedback

Close the loop

• Exit ticket: one deduction and one polite request per learner.

• Revisit the deduction ladder at the start of Lesson 5 (modal review warm-up).

• Collect the negotiation decisions if you need a written accuracy sample.

Feedback for this lesson's speaking

During the negotiation, only tick politeness and strength on the tally; give the detailed modal-strength feedback in the three-minute repair afterwards, using learners' own lines.

LESSON 5 · CONDITIONALS FOR DECISIONS AND POSSIBILITIES — TEACHER GUIDE

Part 3 — Think Beyond the Present | Speaking goal: talk about consequences, alternatives and hypothetical situations accurately

This guide mirrors the Student Book lesson exactly: the same eight functions, the same practice items and the same answers. Follow the parts in order; adapt the timing to your class.

Lesson outcomes and measurable success criteria

By the end of the lesson

• Build accurate zero, first, second, third and mixed conditional sentences in speech.

• Select the conditional type that matches real vs unreal time in a decision task.

• Give hypothetical advice and past reflection using the correct forms.

Success criteria — the learner can:

✓ all five types appear correctly in oral drill or story chain

✓ if-clauses about the future use present simple without will

✓ the Real Talk decision includes a first, a second, and a third or mixed conditional

Materials and preparation

Before the lesson

• Board timeline: NOW-FACT · NOW-UNLIKELY · PAST-NEVER · PAST→NOW.

• Colour-coded if-clause / main-clause cards (optional but effective).

• Formula Book card 5 for display during practice.

Suggested timing (60-minute lesson)

Lesson part

Minutes

The Speaking Hook

4

The Simple Rule

8

See the Difference

3

Practice the Pattern

10

Pair Speaking

11

The Advanced Upgrade

9

Real Talk Challenge

10

Review and Self-Check

5

Total

60

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

• Quick round: pairs answer the three hook conditionals aloud — notice which verb shapes they already produce.

• Collect one answer of each type on the board before teaching anything.

• Tell learners the lesson names and tunes what they just attempted.

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

• Teach Rules 1–3 as one family: real (zero/first) → unreal now (second) → unreal past (third) → mixed. Use each Examples line as choral drill.

• Rule 4 variations: unless / provided / formal should-inversion — read once, drill 'unless' only.

• Stress the will-in-if-clause qualification from the remember line: willingness will is possible; ordinary future conditions take present simple.

Check understanding — quick, whole-class

• 'If it will rain' — acceptable for ordinary future? (no; willingness only) rebuild it.

• Call a type ('mixed!') — pairs produce a sentence within five seconds.

• 'unless' sentence from the class — confirm no double negative.

Part 3 · See the Difference

• Second vs third table: pairs transform the two rows aloud and state the time difference ('now' vs 'then').

• Type 3 vs mixed: ask 'Where is the result?' for each sentence — past or present.

• One-minute board race: learners sort five sentences under the four timeline headings.

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

• Practice A (6): individual (4 minutes) + pair check; A3/A4 must be read aloud with full forms.

• Practice B (6): transformations spoken in pairs; B5 and B6 are open — take two samples.

• Key display; for any will-in-if error, pause and re-run Rule 1's remember line.

Answer key — Practice A and B (identical to the Student Book key)

Practice A. 1 heat / boils · 2 rains / will cancel (or: 'll cancel) · 3 were / would apologise · 4 had left / wouldn't have missed · 5 knew / would call · 6 will go / stays

Practice B. 1 Unless you register, you can't attend. · 2 If he had studied, he wouldn't have failed. · 3 If she had saved money, she could buy the car now. / …would be able to buy… · 4 If I have time, I will help you. · 5 answers vary · 6 answers vary

Where learners lose marks — teaching notes

• A3 'were / would apologise' — 'If I were you' is the standard advice frame; accept 'was' informally but keep 'were' as the taught model.

• A5 'knew / would call' — present unreal; 'would' belongs in the main clause only.

• B2 accepts 'If he had studied, he wouldn't have failed' — learners often add 'so' — explain that if and so do not coexist in one clause pair.

• B3 accepts 'could buy' or 'would be able to buy' — both correct for the past→present mixed type.

• B5/B6 are open: accept any coherent second conditional advice or prize answer that keeps if-clause present simple.

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

• Chain game: start the printed opening; each learner adds one sentence within five seconds (keeps it unscripted).

• Tally types used per pair; demand one third and one mixed before finishing.

• Second chain only if the first ran smoothly; otherwise set it as the extension.

Model exchange for rehearsal (one possible version)

A: If I had woken up early, I would have caught the first bus. B: If I had caught the first bus, I would have arrived before the rain. A: If it had rained all morning, the streets would have flooded — and if I had been at work, I would be tired now. B: If I were you, I'd check the weather before travelling tomorrow.

Part 6 · The Advanced Upgrade

• Intermediate base: one living example per type, then short-form drills aloud (If I'd… / we wouldn't have…).

• Advanced upgrade: inverted conditionals, 'but for', and 'suppose…' — produce one each, then judge which register they fit.

• Discussion: which of the three sounds most formal, and where would you use it?

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

• Planning: learners assign conditional jobs exactly as the plan box instructs.

• One minute of speech to a partner; partners listen for the three required types with the feedback ticks.

• Model uncovered; pairs compare the model's choices (first/second/third-mixed) with their own, then re-deliver one improved line.

Model response (as printed in the Student Book)

If we choose training, the team will improve their skills, but we will have to postpone the equipment purchase. New equipment would help more in the short term, although if I were on the committee, I would invest in people first. If I had been on it last year, I would have set aside a training budget monthly — then we wouldn't be choosing one thing over another now. So my choice is training, and I'd approve it today.

Assessing this open-ended task

• The feedback ticks (first/second/third-mixed/logic) are the assessment — count types heard, do not score grammar mid-speech.

• Accept any logically consistent chain; the model is one path through the task.

• If mixed conditionals dominate wrongly, note it and re-drill the type-3 form in the review phase.

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

• Covered page: one example of each of the five types (choral then individual).

• Turn a real regret into a third conditional — two volunteers.

• Self-check; unticked boxes redo the matching A items.

Differentiation: Intermediate and Advanced pathways

Intermediate — scaffolding and remediation

• Timeline board stays visible; learners point to the time before choosing the form.

• Frames: 'If I had + past perfect, I would have + participle' on a desk card.

• Remediation: learners who miss type 3 re-do A4 and B2 aloud before the Real Talk Challenge.

Advanced — extension and discussion guidance

• Discussion: 'Had I known…' vs 'If I had known…' — where does inversion belong?

• Upgrade: 'But for your help…' replacing a full if-clause; two true examples.

• Register check: which of unless / provided / should you require fits a contract vs a text?

Common learner errors and targeted correction

Expect these — and fix them like this

• 'If it will rain…' → 'If it rains…' — fix: future-in-if drill with five verbs; mention willingness will only if asked.

• 'If I would have known' → 'If I had known' — fix: main-clause-only-would sorting exercise.

• 'unless you don't hurry' → 'unless you hurry' — fix: unless = if not; learners expand three unless sentences both ways.

Shorter-session adaptation (45 minutes)

Keep the objective, cut the load

• Parts 1–4 at 15 + 10; the chain runs one round of six sentences.

• Upgrade task becomes homework (one inverted conditional).

• Real Talk: first option only (training/equipment/trip consequences) — the past reflection moves to the self-check prompt.

Review, consolidation and feedback

Close the loop

• Exit ticket: one third conditional about today.

• Formula card 5 is the revision sheet for Test 2 — point learners to it now.

• Rehearse mixed conditionals again before Review Test 2 (they appear there).

Feedback for this lesson's speaking

During chains, correct only form collapses that block the listener; otherwise collect two errors per chain and repair them as a class puzzle afterwards.

LESSON 6 · WISHES, REGRETS, AND HYPOTHETICAL SITUATIONS — TEACHER GUIDE

Part 3 — Think Beyond the Present | Speaking goal: express preferences, dissatisfaction, regrets and imagined alternatives naturally

This guide mirrors the Student Book lesson exactly: the same eight functions, the same practice items and the same answers. Follow the parts in order; adapt the timing to your class.

Lesson outcomes and measurable success criteria

By the end of the lesson

• Express present wishes, past regrets and preferences with accurate verb forms.

• Use would rather and it's time with correct tense patterns in speech.

• Deliver a one-minute regret-and-advice turn using both wish types.

Success criteria — the learner can:

✓ wish + past vs wish + past perfect chosen correctly in 4 of 5 spoken examples

✓ would rather matches subject and tense in both personal and interpersonal cases

✓ the Real Talk response contains one past regret, one present wish, and advice

Materials and preparation

Before the lesson

• Board: WISH-NOW (past) · WISH-THEN (past perfect) · WANT-CHANGE (would/could).

• Optional: complaint slips (studies, work, health) for pairs who stall.

• Formula Book card 6 for display.

Suggested timing (60-minute lesson)

Lesson part

Minutes

The Speaking Hook

4

The Simple Rule

8

See the Difference

3

Practice the Pattern

10

Pair Speaking

12

The Advanced Upgrade

8

Real Talk Challenge

10

Review and Self-Check

5

Total

60

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

• Learners complete the three hook stems honestly and read them to a partner.

• Sort three class examples on the board under now/then/ability.

• Set the aim: natural regrets without long if-sentences.

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

• Rule 1: present wish; drill the 'time steps back one level' idea with 'I wish I knew' (but I don't).

• Rule 2: regret with past perfect; pair it with 'If only…!' for emotion.

• Rule 3: would rather and it's time as a two-line formula; chorally drill 'It's high time we started.'

• Rule 4: prefer and as if/as though — one real vs unreal example each.

Check understanding — quick, whole-class

• 'I wish I have more time' — repair it live. (had)

• Call the time ('past regret!') — learners fire a wish sentence instantly.

• 'I'd rather you don't' — fix it together. (didn't)

Part 3 · See the Difference

• Table 1: pairs transform present wish ↔ past regret and state the time.

• could vs would: contrast 'I wish I could come' with 'I wish you would come' — me/you and ability/willingness.

• 'It's time' three shapes: read aloud, then learners produce their own for a real situation (late meeting, unpaid bill).

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

• Practice A (6) solo with pair check; A3/A4 (as if / it's high time) need the pattern named aloud.

• Practice B (6): spoken rewrites in pairs; B6 is open — take two samples.

• Key display; drill the wish-past-perfect form if A2 was widely missed.

Answer key — Practice A and B (identical to the Student Book key)

Practice A. 1 knew · 2 hadn't said · 3 owned · 4 made · 5 didn't tell · 6 were

Practice B. 1 I wish I had studied harder. · 2 I'd rather you didn't smoke here. / I'd rather you didn't smoke. · 3 I wish I had more time. · 4 It's time we went. · 5 reading / watching · 6 answers vary

Where learners lose marks — teaching notes

• A4 'made' — it's (high) time + past form, not present; the meaning is 'we are late'.

• A6 'were' — traditional subjunctive; accept 'was' informally but keep 'were' as the careful model, as the lesson states.

• B3: the correction changes the verb to 'had' — learners should explain the present unreal meaning.

• B4 'It's time we went' — accept 'It's time we left/go'? No: bare 'go' is not the pattern taught; keep went/left.

• B5 'reading / watching' — parallel patterns; both must match in form.

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

• Complaint-and-fix: model one complaint-response pair first, then set the two-minute rounds.

• Swap roles on signal; tally wish forms and solution modals.

• Two pairs perform the best complaint-fix exchange for the class.

Model exchange for rehearsal (one possible version)

A: I wish I had more time for my health — I work late every day. B: We are in the same boat. Have you tried shorter workouts? A: I wish I could explain it to my manager. B: It's high time we told him — would you like me to come with you? A: Thanks, but I'd rather you didn't; I want to handle it myself.

Part 6 · The Advanced Upgrade

• Intermediate base: learners sort their own real regrets into now/then and say each aloud.

• Advanced upgrade: 'If only…!' for emotion, diplomatic wish+would in professional English, and 'as though nothing had happened' narrative.

• Discussion: when does 'I wish you would' cross from request into complaint?

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

• Planning per the plan box: real regret, present wish, advice — verb forms decided first.

• One minute to a partner; feedback ticks listened for, no interruption.

• Model uncovered; learners underline the two wish forms in it, then compare with their own structure.

Model response (as printed in the Student Book)

I wish I had taken English seriously at school — I lost two years worrying about mistakes instead of speaking. I wish I could explain things as clearly as my teacher could. What it taught me is this: accuracy grows through use. If I were talking to a younger learner now, I'd say record yourself every week and compare the recordings after a month — the progress is real, and you will hear it.

Assessing this open-ended task

• Assess with the four printed criteria: correct wish forms, natural solutions, genuine tone, both roles completed.

• Accept any complaint topic that uses the target forms; the model is not the only content.

• If present/past wishes keep mixing, run the now/then board sort before the review phase.

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

• Covered: one present wish + one past regret from each learner (round-robin).

• Preference about self vs about partner — two volunteers.

• Self-check; unticked boxes redo A1/A2 and B3 aloud.

Differentiation: Intermediate and Advanced pathways

Intermediate — scaffolding and remediation

• Verb-form frame on the desk: 'wish + past = now · wish + had + participle = then'.

• Complaint starters: 'I wish I had more time for…' · 'I wish I could…'

• Remediation: learners redo B1 and B3 as oral drills before the Real Talk Challenge.

Advanced — extension and discussion guidance

• Discussion: 'We were hoping the report would be ready' — wish or complaint? Which structure and why?

• Upgrade: narrate one line with 'She greeted me as though we had argued yesterday.'

• Register: compare 'I wish you'd be quiet' with 'Would you mind keeping it down?' — when is each appropriate?

Common learner errors and targeted correction

Expect these — and fix them like this

• 'I wish I have more time.' → 'I wish I had more time.' — fix: unreal present takes past form; five-verb flash repair.

• 'I'd rather you don't smoke' → 'didn't' — fix: someone else's action takes the past form; contrast with 'I'd rather stay'.

• 'It's time we will go.' → 'It's time we went.' — fix: no will inside it's time; two examples drilled.

Shorter-session adaptation (45 minutes)

Keep the objective, cut the load

• Parts 1–4 at 15 + 10; complaint round runs two areas, not four.

• Upgrade becomes the self-check homework line.

• Real Talk: 45-second version with a written plan only (no second attempt).

Review, consolidation and feedback

Close the loop

• Exit ticket: one regret and one preference said aloud.

• Flag wish forms for Review Test 2 (items A2/A6 test exactly these).

• Formula card 6 as the revision sheet.

Feedback for this lesson's speaking

Reacts to meaning first ('That sounded like a real regret') — this is a lesson where tone matters; then fix forms in the repair phase, choosing only the one error that appeared most often.

LESSON 7 · COMPARISONS BEYOND THE BASICS — TEACHER GUIDE

Part 4 — Compare and Persuade | Speaking goal: compare clearly and support comparisons with reasons

This guide mirrors the Student Book lesson exactly: the same eight functions, the same practice items and the same answers. Follow the parts in order; adapt the timing to your class.

Lesson outcomes and measurable success criteria

By the end of the lesson

• Form comparatives, superlatives and equality patterns accurately in speech.

• Add degree words and reasons to make comparisons persuasive.

• Build a one-minute persuasion talk containing three accurate comparisons.

Success criteria — the learner can:

✓ no double comparatives and no then/than confusion across the lesson

✓ every comparison in the pair task is supported by a reason

✓ at least two degree words used (far, much, slightly, by far…)

Materials and preparation

Before the lesson

• Board: -er/-est vs more/most decision line, plus irregulars good/better/best.

• Optional: three real items to compare (two phones, two routes, two courses).

• Formula Book card 7 for display.

Suggested timing (60-minute lesson)

Lesson part

Minutes

The Speaking Hook

5

The Simple Rule

7

See the Difference

3

Practice the Pattern

10

Pair Speaking

12

The Advanced Upgrade

8

Real Talk Challenge

10

Review and Self-Check

5

Total

60

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

• Pairs complete the two comparison frames aloud with reasons.

• Take two examples; underline the connector 'because'.

• State the lesson rule: a comparison without a reason is only an opinion.

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

• Rule 1: decision line short/long + irregulars; learners sort five adjectives aloud.

• Rule 2: as…as and the more…the more — drill the printed examples as chunks.

• Rule 3: degree words with meaning nuance (far vs slightly) — read the examples, learners mimic the emphasis.

Check understanding — quick, whole-class

• 'more better' — thumbs down; repair chorally.

• Adjective flash (big / expensive / good): instant comparative form from the class.

• 'better then that' — spot the error in one second (than).

Part 3 · See the Difference

• Comparative vs superlative table: pairs explain the difference for each row in their own words.

• Subtle patterns: 'The sooner, the better' vs 'Sooner or later' — ask what each promises.

• Equality vs near-equality: choral drill 'almost as…as'.

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

• Practice A (6): solo then pair; A2 superlative needs 'the' and irregular form.

• Practice B (6): spoken transformations; B3 and B6 require a spoken reason.

• Key display; run the 'more taller' repair chorus if B2 was missed.

Answer key — Practice A and B (identical to the Student Book key)

Practice A. 1 shorter · 2 the worst · 3 more / faster · 4 more beautifully · 5 as / as · 6 most talented

Practice B. 1 The new laptop is twice as expensive as the old one. · 2 She is taller than me. · 3 This method is far better than that one because it saves time. (answers vary) · 4 answers vary · 5 This is better than that. · 6 answers vary

Where learners lose marks — teaching notes

• A2 'the worst' — superlative with 'of my life' requires 'the'; irregular bad → worst.

• A4 'more beautifully' — adverb comparative uses more (beautifully is long); learners often keep 'beautiful' — clarify adjective vs adverb here.

• B1 'twice as expensive as' — the pattern is as + adj + as with the multiple before the first as.

• B3/B6 are open: accept any far/much/a lot + comparative + because-reason, and any coherent three-city comparison using both forms.

• B5 correction is only than (not then) — the meaning is untouched.

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

• Recommendation game: 30 seconds prep each, then defend; monitor for degree words with a tally.

• Force the joint decision: pairs must agree and justify the agreement.

• Two recommendations played back for class feedback against criteria.

Model exchange for rehearsal (one possible version)

A: Online learning is far more flexible than classroom courses because I can study after work. B: True, but classroom courses are more expensive than online ones and still worth it for discussion. A: It is the feedback that makes the difference — compared with last year, our class has doubled its speaking time. B: The more we practise online, the more confident we become; to sum up, blended learning is best.

Part 6 · The Advanced Upgrade

• Intermediate base: irregulars and degree-word sentences about real life.

• Advanced upgrade: 'by far / the single most…', concessive comparison, and 'compared with' data framing — one of each.

• Discussion: which sounds more academic — 'prices have doubled' or 'compared with 2020, participation has doubled'?

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

• Planning: three comparisons + reasons as printed; keywords only.

• One minute to a partner; listeners count comparisons heard.

• Model uncovered; learners highlight its degree words, then upgrade one of their own sentences with 'far' or 'by far'.

Model response (as printed in the Student Book)

The best age to start learning a language is early childhood — children pick up pronunciation far more easily than adults, and they are much less afraid of mistakes. The best use of one hour a day, however, is deliberate speaking practice: it is twice as effective as passive review because you get instant feedback. Compared with grammar drills alone, conversation is by far the most useful investment. The more you speak, the more natural your grammar becomes.

Assessing this open-ended task

• Count comparisons and reasons with the ticks; a comparison without a reason does not count.

• Accept any topic pair; the joint decision must be stated aloud with at least one degree word.

• Note adjective/adverb slips (beautiful vs beautifully) for the repair phase rather than interrupting.

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

• Covered: one 'far' comparison, one 'the more…the more' sentence.

• Rank three personal things with superlatives + reasons — round-robin.

• Self-check; unticked boxes redo A1/A2 and B2 aloud.

Differentiation: Intermediate and Advanced pathways

Intermediate — scaffolding and remediation

• Adjective decision card: short (-er) vs long (more) with five worked examples.

• Reason frames: '…because it saves time' · '…especially when…'

• Remediation: learners redo A3 and B2 aloud before Real Talk if the pattern slipped.

Advanced — extension and discussion guidance

• Discussion: when does 'arguably the best' beat 'the best'? (evidence vs assertion)

• Upgrade: concessive comparison — 'Although X is cheaper, Y is better value over time.'

• Data talk: describe one real figure ('Compared with last year, enrolment has grown by a third').

Common learner errors and targeted correction

Expect these — and fix them like this

• 'more taller' → 'taller' — fix: double-comparative sort with six adjectives.

• 'better then' → 'better than' — fix: than = comparison, then = time; quick sentence pair.

• Comparing price with quality — fix: like-for-like rule; learners repair one mixed comparison.

Shorter-session adaptation (45 minutes)

Keep the objective, cut the load

• Parts 1–4 at 15 + 10; recommendation game takes one presentation each, decision included.

• Upgrade becomes a written finisher task.

• Real Talk: choose ONE prompt topic; still three comparisons with reasons.

Review, consolidation and feedback

Close the loop

• Exit ticket: one far/much + comparative about the school or city.

• Comparisons feed Lessons 8 and 15 (persuasion and hedging) — revisit in Test 2 preparation.

• Formula card 7 for revision.

Feedback for this lesson's speaking

During presentations, tick comparisons and reasons separately — the split shows learners which half they are missing; repair adjective/adverb choices afterwards with three class-built examples.

LESSON 8 · LINKING IDEAS AND BUILDING ARGUMENTS — TEACHER GUIDE

Part 4 — Compare and Persuade | Speaking goal: organise opinions into coherent, well-linked spoken arguments

This guide mirrors the Student Book lesson exactly: the same eight functions, the same practice items and the same answers. Follow the parts in order; adapt the timing to your class.

Lesson outcomes and measurable success criteria

By the end of the lesson

• Link ideas with the correct linker family (contrast, cause, result, purpose).

• Deliver a short argument with point → reason → example → summary structure.

• Use one concession and one counterpoint without breaking grammar rules.

Success criteria — the learner can:

✓ despite + noun/-ing and although + clause both used correctly at least twice

✓ the spoken argument contains all four skeleton parts

✓ the closing summary opens with a printed summariser

Materials and preparation

Before the lesson

• Board: four linker families in four columns (contrast / cause / result / addition).

• Skeleton strip: POINT → REASON → EXAMPLE → LINK/SUMMARY.

• Optional: debate motion written before class ('Homework should be replaced…').

Suggested timing (60-minute lesson)

Lesson part

Minutes

The Speaking Hook

4

The Simple Rule

8

See the Difference

3

Practice the Pattern

10

Pair Speaking

11

The Advanced Upgrade

9

Real Talk Challenge

10

Review and Self-Check

5

Total

60

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

• 30-second talk on 'Why people learn English', then partner counts the linkers used.

• Tally class linkers in the four columns.

• Name today's aim: not more linkers — the right linkers, in the right slot.

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

• Rule 1: contrast/concession — build although vs despite on the board from one idea: 'Although it rained' / 'Despite the rain'.

• Rule 2: cause/result — clause vs noun pairs; drill because vs because of.

• Rule 3: the argument skeleton — say the printed example as a script once, then learners rebuild it from four keywords.

• Rule 4: summarisers — choral drill of four closers.

Check understanding — quick, whole-class

• 'Despite of' — repair live and keep it on the board as the lesson's anti-example.

• Call a family ('result!') — learners shout two linkers from it.

• 'Although the cost…' — rebuild as despite or although-clause, both acceptable if grammatical.

Part 3 · See the Difference

• Three-package table (although / despite / however): learners repack one idea three ways aloud.

• because vs because of: instant transformation round.

• while/whereas vs although: ask which one concedes — connect to Lesson 7's comparison language.

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

• Practice A (6): solo + pairs; A2 (Despite being…) is the known trap — justify the choice.

• Practice B (6): B4/B6 spoken skeletons; B4 must literally contain point, reason, example.

• Key display; run the 'despite of' repair chorus unconditionally.

Answer key — Practice A and B (identical to the Student Book key)

Practice A. 1 Despite · 2 Despite (not 'although' — it needs a clause: Although she was very tired) · 3 however · 4 so that · 5 As a result · 6 whereas

Practice B. 1 Although the task was difficult, everyone finished. · 2 Despite not being selected, she applied again. / Despite the rejection, she applied again. · 3 Despite the cost, we decided to proceed. · 4 answers vary — must include point, reason, example · 5 Despite the cost, we bought it. / Although it was costly, we bought it. · 6 answers vary — must open with To sum up / All in all / In conclusion

Where learners lose marks — teaching notes

• A2 'Despite' — 'being very tired' is -ing, not a clause; accept the full 'Although she was very tired' only if the learner restructures.

• A5 'As a result' — result of cancellation; 'Although' would invert the logic.

• B4 must visibly contain point + reason + example — the key allows variation but not missing parts.

• B6 requires a printed summariser opener (To sum up / All in all / In conclusion) — any content after it is open.

• B3/B5 both accept the two grammatical repairs listed; if a class prefers 'Although the cost was high', it is equally correct — say so aloud.

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

• Mini-debate: positions drawn or assigned; two minutes per side, then swap.

• Monitor with the four required linker slots as a checklist.

• Require the closing summary and the joint verdict line.

Model exchange for rehearsal (one possible version)

A: I believe homework should be replaced by daily speaking practice. B: Although speaking is important, homework teaches discipline. A: Despite the need for discipline, speaking every day builds fluency faster. B: However, many learners skip daily tasks. A: Therefore we need scheduled speaking slots, not less homework. To sum up, add speaking without removing homework.

Part 6 · The Advanced Upgrade

• Intermediate base: sort ten linkers into the four families under time pressure.

• Advanced upgrade: 'Not only… but also' with inversion, concessive balance ('Admittedly… even so…'), and clause-commenting 'which'.

• Discussion: why is 'which changed the whole mood' more elegant than a second sentence?

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

• Planning: claim, two reasons, concession, linkers — keywords as printed.

• 90 seconds to a partner without notes; listeners follow the skeleton on paper.

• Model uncovered; mark its four skeleton parts, then compare with the listener's notes of the learner's own talk.

Model response (as printed in the Student Book)

I believe what makes a good teacher is clear feedback. This is because learners improve fastest when they know exactly what to fix. For instance, my first English teacher corrected our pronunciation every day, and within a month our class sounded noticeably better. Although games and fun activities help people relax, I would trade them for precise correction any day. To sum up: a good teacher makes the next step obvious.

Assessing this open-ended task

• Checklist per side: four linker slots filled, skeleton visible, counterargument answered, summary spoken.

• Argument quality is judged by structure and clarity, not by the position defended.

• If despite + clause keeps occurring, stop after the round and rebuild it with the whole class.

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

• Covered: a 20-second argument with exactly three linkers (count them).

• Same contrast idea three ways: although / despite / however.

• Self-check; unticked boxes redo A1/A2 and B3 aloud.

Differentiation: Intermediate and Advanced pathways

Intermediate — scaffolding and remediation

• Four-column board stays visible; learners point to the column before speaking.

• Frames: 'Although…, …' · 'Despite + noun, …' · 'This is because…' · 'To sum up…'

• Remediation: pairs re-do B2 and B3 aloud before Real Talk if their debate showed the error.

Advanced — extension and discussion guidance

• Discussion: 'It is true that…; nevertheless…' — who are you conceding to? Build one about the debate motion.

• Upgrade: clause-commenting 'which' — two learners describe a manager who apologised.

• Precision: compare 'however' vs 'nevertheless' — strength and position in the sentence.

Common learner errors and targeted correction

Expect these — and fix them like this

• 'Despite of the cost' → 'Despite the cost / In spite of the cost' — fix: two-slot board (despite | in spite of) + noun card.

• 'Although the cost, we bought it' → 'Despite the cost…' or 'Although it was costly…' — fix: clause-or-noun sorter.

• Arguments that list opinions without reasons — fix: skeleton strip visible during every speaking task from now on.

Shorter-session adaptation (45 minutes)

Keep the objective, cut the load

• Parts 1–4 at 15 + 10; debate runs one side only plus a 30-second rebuttal.

• Upgrade task moves to the advanced homework sheet.

• Real Talk: 60-second talk; summary still required.

Review, consolidation and feedback

Close the loop

• Exit ticket: one although sentence and one despite sentence about today.

• The argument skeleton returns in Lessons 15–16 and the Final Assessment speaking task.

• Formula card 8 for revision before Test 2.

Feedback for this lesson's speaking

Tick the four linker slots during speeches — visible progress keeps motivation; repair the contrast family after the debate with two anonymous sentences, one corrected live.

LESSON 9 · PASSIVE VOICE IN NATURAL ENGLISH — TEACHER GUIDE

Part 5 — Describe and Explain | Speaking goal: choose between active and passive for the right focus

This guide mirrors the Student Book lesson exactly: the same eight functions, the same practice items and the same answers. Follow the parts in order; adapt the timing to your class.

Lesson outcomes and measurable success criteria

By the end of the lesson

• Build accurate passive forms across tenses and choose active or passive for the right focus.

• Use one reporting structure (It is said / believed that …) in a short news brief.

• Explain to a listener when the agent is kept and when it is omitted.

Success criteria — the learner can:

✓ at least 5 of 6 Practice A passive forms correct without prompting

✓ the newsroom exchange includes two passives and one reporting structure

✓ listeners confirm the tone sounds objective, not personal

Materials and preparation

Before the lesson

• Board: PASSIVE = be + past participle — tense lives in 'be' (is/are/was/were/will be/has been).

• News prompts ready: accident, opening, rule change, sports result.

• Formula Book card 9 for display.

Suggested timing (60-minute lesson)

Lesson part

Minutes

The Speaking Hook

4

The Simple Rule

7

See the Difference

4

Practice the Pattern

10

Pair Speaking

12

The Advanced Upgrade

8

Real Talk Challenge

10

Review and Self-Check

5

Total

60

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

• Display the two bicycle sentences side-by-side. Elicit: whose story is each one?

• Pairs produce one active and one passive version of a real event from their week.

• Take two pairs' answers and mark which focuses on the result.

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

• Rule 1: passive formation across tenses — chorally read the four lines, then transform one sentence through every tense.

• Rule 2: when to use it — ask 'Who cares about the doer here?' for each Examples line.

• Rule 3: reporting verbs — drill the It-is-said pair aloud.

Check understanding — quick, whole-class

• Board transform: 'They clean the office every day.' → learners say the passive.

• 'My phone was broken by me' — natural? (no — use the active)

• Reporting pair quick-fire: 'People say that he is the best.' → two passive versions.

Part 3 · See the Difference

• Active vs passive table: cover the right column, pairs guess the rule, then reveal.

• Get-passive contrast — mark the emotion tag and give one informal get example.

• False passives: read two on the board; ask why they are not real passives.

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

• Practice A (6) solo + pair check; insist on full forms including auxiliaries.

• Practice B (6): B1–B3 spoken transformations in pairs; B4–B6 corrections aloud.

• Key after checking; drill any tense error by walking the verb through the four tenses.

Answer key — Practice A and B (identical to the Student Book key)

Practice A. 1 was built · 2 will be announced · 3 is cleaned · 4 was stolen · 5 has just been introduced · 6 be sent

Practice B. 1 My bicycle has been stolen. · 2 The board made the decision. · 3 It is said that he is the best candidate. / He is said to be the best candidate. · 4 The house was built in 1990. · 5 I lost my phone. / I had my phone stolen. (answers vary) · 6 The road will be closed tomorrow.

Where learners lose marks — teaching notes

• A5 'has just been introduced' — adverb position before the participle; 'has just introduced' would be active and wrong.

• B3 accepts either 'It is said that he is the best' or 'He is said to be…'.

• B5 'I lost my phone' — insist on the natural active; 'I had my phone stolen' is also credited where noted.

• B2 'The board made the decision' — learners must restore the agent as subject; 'It was decided' would need a different structure.

• B6 is open only within the passive requirement — insist on one future passive with when/tomorrow.

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

• Newsroom: assign reporter/editor; three events each, passives in report style.

• Editor question 'Who did it?' forces the agent decision.

• Swap roles in the second round.

Model exchange for rehearsal (one possible version)

A: A new library was opened near the hospital. B: Who opened it? A: The mayor opened it, but it is said that funding came from abroad. B: How about a rule change? A: Smoking has been banned on campus — students were informed this morning. B: Was anyone upset? A: A few were, but the meeting was held calmly.

Part 6 · The Advanced Upgrade

• Intermediate base: passive in four tenses from objects in the room + reporting pair.

• Advanced upgrade: get-promoted example, alleged/assumed, and participle tail in speech — one of each.

• Discussion: where does the passive improve credibility (reports, data)?

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

• Planning as printed: three events — two about the result, one for comment — tenses fixed.

• 90 seconds to a partner; covered model until after one attempt.

• Uncover the model; compare passive count and final active comment, then re-deliver one improved sentence.

Model response (as printed in the Student Book)

Three things happened this week. A new footbridge was opened near the school, so traffic has been diverted along the main road. It is said that the council will publish the survey results on Friday, and two main streets were cleaned every night last week. My own view is simple: the council should publish the data openly — that is the first thing I would ask for.

Assessing this open-ended task

• Passives counted live against the four criteria; objective tone means no first-person story.

• Accept any news content that holds the structure; the model is one of many.

• If reporting structure is missing, prompt once with 'People say…' → 'It is said…'.

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

• Covered: three objects from the room into passives (different tenses).

• Formal reporting sentence about a known person — volunteer round.

• Self-check; unticked boxes redo Practice A and B4 aloud.

Differentiation: Intermediate and Advanced pathways

Intermediate — scaffolding and remediation

• Tense table stays visible during pair work; learners point before speaking.

• Frames: 'was/were done' · 'is/are done' · 'will be done' · 'It is said that…'
