• Remediation: re-do B4 (builted → built) as a choral correction before Real Talk.

Advanced — extension and discussion guidance

• Get-passive in speech: 'He got promoted' vs 'He was promoted' — feeling marked?

• Reporting nuance: alleged vs claimed — which accuses more strongly?

• Formal tail: 'Founded in 1971, the school…' — one own example.

Common learner errors and targeted correction

Expect these — and fix them like this

• 'The house was builted' → 'was built' — fix: irregular participle sort.

• 'My phone was stolen by me' → 'I lost my phone' — fix: active for your own actions.

• Keeping the agent when the event matters more — fix: agent-last rule; give the agent only if asked.

Shorter-session adaptation (45 minutes)

Keep the objective, cut the load

• Parts 1–4 at 15 + 10; newsroom runs two items instead of three.

• Upgrade moves to homework; reporting pair kept in class.

• Real Talk: two events only, still with one reporting structure and final active comment.

Review, consolidation and feedback

Close the loop

• Exit ticket: one passive from each of two tenses about today.

• Passive feeds Lessons 10, 13–14 and the Final Assessment (A5/B5).

• Formula card 9.

Feedback for this lesson's speaking

Tick passives and reporting structures without interrupting the report-style delivery; repair the tense of be only after the brief, with two anonymous examples.

LESSON 10 · CAUSATIVE STRUCTURES — TEACHER GUIDE

Part 5 — Describe and Explain | Speaking goal: talk about services, arrangements, influence and responsibility naturally

This guide mirrors the Student Book lesson exactly: the same eight functions, the same practice items and the same answers. Follow the parts in order; adapt the timing to your class.

Lesson outcomes and measurable success criteria

By the end of the lesson

• Use have/get something done to arrange services and to describe misfortunes.

• Distinguish make, let, have and get + person + verb in speech.

• Negotiate a service conversation that includes causative language and a price/time agreement.

Success criteria — the learner can:

✓ causative service vs accident distinction correct in at least 4 of 5 attempts

✓ make/let/have/get verb patterns used correctly (to only after get)

✓ negotiation ends with a stated time and price

Materials and preparation

Before the lesson

• Board: HAVE/GET + object + participle = service OR accident.

• Service vocabulary ready: haircuts, repairs, tailoring, deliveries, cleaning.

• Formula Book card 10.

Suggested timing (60-minute lesson)

Lesson part

Minutes

The Speaking Hook

5

The Simple Rule

7

See the Difference

3

Practice the Pattern

10

Pair Speaking

12

The Advanced Upgrade

8

Real Talk Challenge

10

Review and Self-Check

5

Total

60

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

• Hook conversation: what do people 'have done' in your city? — collect five examples on the board.

• Ask who does it (self vs hired) for each — mark S or H.

• Tell learners the lesson names this structure.

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

• Rule 1: have/get sth done — chorally read, then contrast service vs story-misfortune examples.

• Rule 2: make/let/have/get + person + verb — sort four sentences by force (force / allow / instruct / persuade).

• Rule 3: service phrases — drill 'I get my…done…every month' as a chunk.

Check understanding — quick, whole-class

• 'I had my phone stolen on the bus.' — is the stealing a service? (no — misfortune) but same grammar.

• Pattern check: make + to? (no) get + to? (yes)

• Board 'get my car to repair' — whole-class repair.

Part 3 · See the Difference

• Service vs accident table: pairs label each row before seeing the Why column.

• Causative-verbs table: read aloud, then learners supply their own 'made me…' sentence.

• Make-passive point: 'I was made to wait' — mark the kept to.

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

• Practice A (6) solo + pair; A3/A6 (made/lost vs persuade) need the pattern named.

• Practice B (6): spoken rewrites; B5 and B6 are open — two samples.

• Key display; on any to-after-make error, stop and rebuild Rule 2.

Answer key — Practice A and B (identical to the Student Book key)

Practice A. 1 altered · 2 cut · 3 lose · 4 use · 5 tested · 6 to eat

Practice B. 1 I had my car serviced. · 2 I got my friend to drive us. / After much discussion, I got my friend to drive. · 3 I will get my car repaired tomorrow. · 4 She made me wait outside. · 5 answers vary · 6 Could you have my phone screen replaced? / How much would it cost to have my screen replaced?

Where learners lose marks — teaching notes

• A3 'lose' — made + base verb, no to; 'made to lose' here would be passive and wrong.

• A6 'to eat' — get needs to; 'eat' alone would be make/have/let.

• B1 'I had my car serviced.' — accept 'got' variant.

• B2 'I got my friend to drive us.' — the persuasion marker to is the whole point.

• B3 correction: 'get my car repaired' (participle, not infinitive). B4: 'made me wait'.

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

• Service shop: A = shop, B = customer with three problems; causatives + price/time.

• Monitor for make/let/get inclusion with a tick; prompt once if missing.

• Swap roles or run a second customer if time allows.

Model exchange for rehearsal (one possible version)

A: I need to have my suit shortened — can you do it this week? B: We can have it ready by Thursday; it will cost 400 afghanis. A: My mother made me wear it to the wedding — I had my shoes repaired too. B: Did your boss let you leave early? A: He got me to finish the report first, then he let me go.

Part 6 · The Advanced Upgrade

• Intermediate base: four causatives from own life + service chunks.

• Advanced upgrade: have-person-do delegation, 'had us laughing', 'got round to…' — one each true.

• Discussion: when is have-person-do businesslike but impolite?

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

• Planning: three moments — arranged service, accident, make/let/get.

• One minute to a partner; model covered.

• Model uncovered; underline the causatives, compare counts, then improve one line.

Model response (as printed in the Student Book)

Last Friday started badly. I had my car serviced the evening before, but it still wouldn't start, so I let my neighbour try the battery — he is a mechanic. Then the courier delivered my laptop to the wrong company, and I had to wait while it was forwarded. My manager made me postpone the presentation until the afternoon, and I finally got my brother to drive me to work. By the evening the whole day had me laughing — what a mess!

Assessing this open-ended task

• Listen for the four printed criteria; time/price agreement is required.

• Misfortune 'had sth done' counts as causative only if learners name it as accident, not service.

• Accept any price vocabulary that closes the negotiation.

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

• Covered: three things to have done this month — each a full causative sentence.

• Made vs let: one person per learner.

• Self-check; unticked redo A1/A6 and B2 aloud.

Differentiation: Intermediate and Advanced pathways

Intermediate — scaffolding and remediation

• Desk card: HAVE/GET + object + done; make/let/have + base / get + to.

• Chunk drill: 'I had my car fixed' · 'I got my friend to help me'.

• Remediation: re-drill A5/A6 before Real Talk if pair work confused to.

Advanced — extension and discussion guidance

• Delegation: 'I'll have the team look into it.' vs 'I'll ask the team to…' — difference?

• Story colour: 'He had us all laughing' — when does it fit?

• End-up pattern: 'I ended up waiting…' as complement to causatives.

Common learner errors and targeted correction

Expect these — and fix them like this

• 'Will get my car to repair' → 'repaired' — fix: have/get + done chorus.

• 'Made me to wait' → 'wait' — fix: make-pattern sort.

• Using have-done for self-done actions — fix: 'I fixed my laptop' vs 'I had it fixed' contrast on the board.

Shorter-session adaptation (45 minutes)

Keep the objective, cut the load

• Parts 1–4 at 15 + 10; negotiation runs two items with price/time.

• Second role in the pair becomes homework dialogue.

• Upgrade moves to the self-check spoken task.

Review, consolidation and feedback

Close the loop

• Exit ticket: one service and one misfortune sentence.

• Causatives return in the Final Assessment (A8/B7); link them there.

• Formula card 10.

Feedback for this lesson's speaking

During the shop role-play, tick causative accuracy and negotiation outcome only; repair a sample of to errors afterwards on the board, one pair at a time.

LESSON 11 · GERUNDS AND INFINITIVES — TEACHER GUIDE

Part 6 — Speak with Greater Precision | Speaking goal: choose the right verb pattern for your meaning

This guide mirrors the Student Book lesson exactly: the same eight functions, the same practice items and the same answers. Follow the parts in order; adapt the timing to your class.

Lesson outcomes and measurable success criteria

By the end of the lesson

• Choose gerund or infinitive correctly after the core lesson verbs.

• Use one meaning-changing verb (remember/forget/stop/try) with both patterns.

• Handle preposition + -ing including look forward to / be used to.

Success criteria — the learner can:

✓ at most two -ing/to errors across the pair interview

✓ one meaning-changing verb used correctly and explained

✓ no 'to + -ing' errors where to is a preposition

Materials and preparation

Before the lesson

• Board: -ING verbs (enjoy, mind, avoid…) vs TO verbs (hope, decide, plan…).

• Meaning-changers ready: stop (quit vs pause) · remember (before vs after) · try.

• Formula Book card 11.

Suggested timing (60-minute lesson)

Lesson part

Minutes

The Speaking Hook

4

The Simple Rule

7

See the Difference

4

Practice the Pattern

10

Pair Speaking

12

The Advanced Upgrade

8

Real Talk Challenge

10

Review and Self-Check

5

Total

60

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

• Learners finish the four hook stems; pairs compare.

• Ask 'Which felt natural with -ing? With to?' — collect five on each side.

• State the aim: -ing after some verbs is not a decoration.

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

• Rule 1: -ing verbs as a group; Rule 2: to verbs as a group — two quick sorts.

• Rule 3: meaning-changing demo: read both I-remember sentences and ask which action came first.

• Rule 4: preposition + -ing — insist 'look forward to + -ing' chorally three times.

Check understanding — quick, whole-class

• Five-verb thumbs: enjoy? (ing) decide? (to) mind? (ing) hope? (to) suggest? (ing)

• 'I stopped to eat' vs 'I stopped eating' — action test: which lunch ended?

• 'look forward to' — following verb is…? (meeting)

Part 3 · See the Difference

• Meaning-changing table: cover the right column; pairs predict, then reveal.

• Need + -ing vs need + to — write both; ask which is more natural in the region.

• Preposition traps: rapid-fire four prompts ('interested in…').

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

• Practice A (6) solo + pair; A4 is the preposition trap — emphasise it.

• Practice B (6): B1–B3 corrections aloud; B5 meaning choice named.

• Key display; if B2 recurs, re-drill look-forward-to with the whole class.

Answer key — Practice A and B (identical to the Student Book key)

Practice A. 1 helping · 2 answering · 3 to accept · 4 hearing · 5 smoking · 6 to open

Practice B. 1 I enjoy reading novels. · 2 I look forward to meeting you. · 3 She suggested going early. · 4 The room needs cleaning. / The room needs to be cleaned. · 5 posting · 6 answers vary

Where learners lose marks — teaching notes

• A4 'hearing' — 'to' is a preposition here; 'to hear' in this frame is the target error.

• A5 'smoking' — 'stopped smoking' = quit; 'stopped to smoke' would be pause-and-smoke.

• A6 'to open' — attempt, not experiment; 'try opening' would be method.

• B3 'suggested going' — 'suggested me to go' is the error this item exists to remove.

• B5 expects the -ing reading for 'I remember calling her'; credit the alternative only if the learner explains the meaning correctly.

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

• Interview: pairs adapt the four printed question frames; use four patterns each.

• One follow-up after most answers required — monitor for interview depth.

• Swap roles; take two strong exchanges to replay for the class.

Model exchange for rehearsal (one possible version)

A: What do you enjoy doing at weekends? B: I enjoy hiking. A: Have you decided to change anything this year? B: I have decided to learn English properly. A: What do you avoid doing? B: I try to avoid complaining — I stopped doing it last year. A: Nice. What are you looking forward to? B: Looking forward to finishing this course!

Part 6 · The Advanced Upgrade

• Intermediate base: five chunks per pattern + meaning-pair drill.

• Advanced upgrade: gerund as subject, 'no point in + -ing / worth + -ing', 'have difficulty + -ing'.

• Discussion: when does 'There is no point…' shut down a debate politely?

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

• Planning: three -ing activities + two to-plans + one meaning-changer marked.

• One minute to a partner; model covered.

• Model uncovered; count the patterns in it, compare with own talk, upgrade one line.

Model response (as printed in the Student Book)

Learning English has taught me to be patient with myself. I enjoy reading in English now, and at first I tried translating every word — that only slowed me down, so I stopped doing it and started guessing from context. I keep a short vocabulary journal every evening because writing helps me notice patterns. I used to avoid speaking because I feared mistakes, so I've decided to join an evening class this winter and speak with real people.

Assessing this open-ended task

• Pattern accuracy decides success — meaning-changer and preposition items are must-pass.

• Follow-ups must be present; interview that lists answers without questioning is incomplete.

• The Real Talk requirement is quantitative: 3× -ing + 2× to + decision sentence.

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

• Covered: two sentences per meaning-changer (stop + try).

• Five verbs per list from memory — pairs compete.

• Self-check; unticked redo A1/A6 and B2 aloud.

Differentiation: Intermediate and Advanced pathways

Intermediate — scaffolding and remediation

• Chunk cards: 'enjoy + ing' · 'decided to + base' · 'look forward to + ing'.

• Starter bank: 'I enjoy…' · 'I decided to…' · 'I avoid…'

• Remediation: if to-preposition slips, re-do A4 and B2 chorally before Real Talk.

Advanced — extension and discussion guidance

• Subject gerund debate: 'Finding time is harder than finding motivation' — true?

• Worth / no-point frames: three opinions about study habits.

• Difficulty frame: 'I had difficulty + -ing' about accent or reading speed.

Common learner errors and targeted correction

Expect these — and fix them like this

• 'Enjoy to read' → 'reading' — fix: -ing-verb list drill.

• 'Look forward to meet' → 'meeting' — fix: preposition-to check; board both uses of to.

• Using only to-patterns — fix: require one -ing sentence per answer in the interview.

Shorter-session adaptation (45 minutes)

Keep the objective, cut the load

• Parts 1–4 at 15 + 10; interview uses three questions instead of four.

• Upgrade patterns become homework examples.

• Real Talk: 45 seconds with the same counting requirement.

Review, consolidation and feedback

Close the loop

• Exit ticket: preposition + -ing about this lesson.

• Test 3 revisits this lesson — flag Appendix 1 card 11.

• Gerund/infinitive feeds Lesson 13's verb patterns (suggest/warn) — connect there.

Feedback for this lesson's speaking

Note the meaning-changing verbs live — one 'stop' correction from a learner's own story teaches more than ten worksheet items; repair the rest after.

LESSON 12 · RELATIVE CLAUSES AND CONCISE DESCRIPTIONS — TEACHER GUIDE

Part 6 — Speak with Greater Precision | Speaking goal: describe people, places and ideas precisely in one sentence

This guide mirrors the Student Book lesson exactly: the same eight functions, the same practice items and the same answers. Follow the parts in order; adapt the timing to your class.

Lesson outcomes and measurable success criteria

By the end of the lesson

• Build accurate defining and non-defining relative clauses in speech.

• Reduce a clause correctly by dropping which-is/who-was where possible.

• Choose who/which/that/whose/where and punctuate meaning accordingly.

Success criteria — the learner can:

✓ relative pronoun choice correct in at least 5 of 6 spoken descriptions

✓ one non-defining clause used with correct meaning and pause

✓ one reduced clause produced naturally in the talk

Materials and preparation

Before the lesson

• Board: who/people · which/things · that/both · whose/possession · where/place.

• Optional: classroom objects to describe without naming.

• Formula Book card 12.

Suggested timing (60-minute lesson)

Lesson part

Minutes

The Speaking Hook

5

The Simple Rule

7

See the Difference

3

Practice the Pattern

10

Pair Speaking

12

The Advanced Upgrade

8

Real Talk Challenge

10

Review and Self-Check

5

Total

60

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

• Guessing hook: learners describe (who/which/that in every sentence) without naming.

• Two strong descriptions played back; class names the pronoun each used.

• Goal stated: two ideas in one clean sentence.

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

• Rule 1: defining — essential, no commas; object pronoun can drop — drill with one sentence each on the board.

• Rule 2: non-defining — extra detail, commas, never that — contrast the same name with/without commas.

• Rule 3: preposition position — formal vs normal vs speech, all three versions of one sentence.

• Rule 4: reduced — drop only who is/which was; wrong drops shown first as anti-examples.

Check understanding — quick, whole-class

• 'My mother, that lives…' — correct? (no: who after commas)

• 'The book what I read' — which pronoun? (that/which, no what)

• Reduced test: can 'who called' become 'man called'? (no — full verb, not droppable)

Part 3 · See the Difference

• Defining vs non-defining table: pairs state 'how many?' for each row.

• that/which/who sorting: speech vs commas rule — three quick examples.

• Whose vs of-whom: why is 'whose' natural and 'of whom' clumsy?

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

• Practice A (6) solo + pair; A2 comma and A5 gap require justification.

• Practice B (6): B1–B5 transformations spoken; B6 performed as a 20-second talk.

• Key display; if A5 is missed, re-teach the reduced rule with the printed example.

Answer key — Practice A and B (identical to the Student Book key)

Practice A. 1 who · 2 which · 3 where · 4 whose · 5 (that) were / which were — or simply 'announced today' with 'The results announced today…' · 6 that (or which)

Practice B. 1 The teacher who taught me last year is excellent. · 2 My friend, who is a pilot, travels constantly. · 3 My mother, who lives in Kandahar, is visiting. · 4 The book (that) I read was amazing. · 5 Students interested in the course should apply. · 6 answers vary

Where learners lose marks — teaching notes

• A2 'which' — commas demand which/who, not that.

• A5 expects the reduced form or explicit 'which were'; both credited; the gap is the lesson's test.

• A6: the omitted pronoun is subject vs object — B6 in student book clarifies it; both 'that' and 'which' credited for the object case.

• B3 accepts only 'who' after commas; 'that' after commas is never correct.

• B6 is open but must demonstrably contain both clause types — do not score a single-clause name.

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

• Guessing game: two items each, defining + non-defining, make the partner guess.

• Second pass: improve the sentences to be more concise — one edit each.

• Class hears the best concise version.

Model exchange for rehearsal (one possible version)

A: The woman who is standing by the window is my colleague — the one who taught me last year. B: The colleague with whom you worked? A: Yes, the colleague I worked with on the project. She, who lives in Bamyan, visits us twice a year. — B: The students interested in the course should apply early; the man whose son won the prize applied yesterday.

Part 6 · The Advanced Upgrade

• Intermediate base: four pronouns drilled + object pronoun dropped.

• Advanced upgrade: which-comment, cleft 'what', reduced in formal register — one each.

• Discussion: 'which surprised everyone' vs 'that surprised everyone' — which is a comment on the whole sentence?

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

• Planning: person → defining role → non-defining extra → reduced description.

• One minute to a partner without notes; model covered.

• Model uncovered; count its four clauses, compare, improve one learner sentence.

Model response (as printed in the Student Book)

The person who influenced me most is my uncle, who taught physics for thirty years. He is the man whose advice I still hear when I sit down to study: start with the hardest task. The teacher who encouraged me at school lent me books written by Afghan authors, and the colleague sitting beside me at my first job showed me how to admit a mistake quickly. Anyone working with him learns the same thing — preparation beats talent.

Assessing this open-ended task

• Criteria in the pair and talk boxes decide — pronoun choice + defining/non-defining meaning + concision.

• Guessing success is the speaking test: if the partner guesses, the description did its job.

• Count the reduced clause in Real Talk explicitly — accept only a droppings of who-is/

• which-was, not a raw participle.

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

• Covered: one defining + one non-defining about the room.

• City description: two + reduced — volunteer then pairs.

• Self-check; unticked redo A1/A4 and B3 aloud.

Differentiation: Intermediate and Advanced pathways

Intermediate — scaffolding and remediation

• Pronoun board visible; learners point before speaking.

• Starters: 'The person who…' · 'The place where…'

• Remediation: if A2/B3 keep failing, drill commas-as-pauses aloud with hand gestures.

Advanced — extension and discussion guidance

• Comment-which: 'She apologised, which changed the whole mood.' — learners build one.

• Cleft focus: 'What I need is time.' — build one about their own study.

• Reduced formality: when does 'Anyone arriving late…' sound sharper than 'If you arrive late…'?

Common learner errors and targeted correction

Expect these — and fix them like this

• 'The book what I read' → 'the book I read' — fix: pronoun chart on desk.

• 'My mother, that…' → 'who' — fix: after a comma, never that.

• Dropping a full verb instead of who is — fix: only who is/which was droppable, shown by two anti-examples.

Shorter-session adaptation (45 minutes)

Keep the objective, cut the load

• Parts 1–4 at 15 + 10; guessing game one item each.

• Advanced upgrades become three written sentences for homework.

• Real Talk: two clause types required instead of three + reduced.

Review, consolidation and feedback

Close the loop

• Exit ticket: 'The person who…which…' about a classmate.

• Relative clauses return in the Final Assessment (C5/C8) — flag those items.

• Formula card 12.

Feedback for this lesson's speaking

Tick clause-type accuracy rather than elegance during descriptions; repair the worst pronoun error on the board afterwards with two correct reformulations.

LESSON 13 · REPORTED SPEECH AND REPORTING VERBS — TEACHER GUIDE

Part 7 — Sound More Natural and Advanced | Speaking goal: report conversations and summarise information accurately and naturally

This guide mirrors the Student Book lesson exactly: the same eight functions, the same practice items and the same answers. Follow the parts in order; adapt the timing to your class.

Lesson outcomes and measurable success criteria

By the end of the lesson

• Report statements, questions and commands with correct backshift and time reference.

• Use reporting verbs beyond say (admit, warn, suggest, remind…) naturally in speech.

• Retell a real conversation with at least four varied reported items and a final comment.

Success criteria — the learner can:

✓ backshift accurate for at least 4 of 5 statements

✓ reported questions use statement order (no do, no inversion)

✓ time words shifted where the reporting is later

Materials and preparation

Before the lesson

• Board: backshift ladder (present → past → past perfect; will→would; can→could).

• Reporting-verb strip: admit/agree/argue/claim/warn/insist/suggest/remind.

• Formula Book card 13.

Suggested timing (60-minute lesson)

Lesson part

Minutes

The Speaking Hook

4

The Simple Rule

7

See the Difference

4

Practice the Pattern

10

Pair Speaking

11

The Advanced Upgrade

9

Real Talk Challenge

10

Review and Self-Check

5

Total

60

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

• Learners report what someone really said to them this week — no reading, no notes.

• Two samples whole-class; mark direct vs reported on the board.

• State the aim: half of adult speaking is reporting — accuracy buys respect.

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

• Rule 1: one-step backshift — chorally walk the ladder with one sentence per step.

• Rule 2: questions/commands — build one Y/N + if and one W(h)-question together on the board.

• Rule 3: reporting verbs as chunks — admit -ing / promised to / warned not to / suggested -ing.

• Rule 4: time shift — two examples only; the 'same-day keep' exception flagged.

Check understanding — quick, whole-class

• 'He said me that…' — fix together. (told me)

• 'She suggested me to go' — fix. (going / that I go)

• Time check: 'tomorrow' → 'the next day' — when can you keep 'tomorrow'?

Part 3 · See the Difference

• say vs tell vs ask table: pairs sort three sentences before revealing the pattern line.

• Same-tense vs backshift table: ask when present tense stays (still true now).

• Command/request/advice row: four force levels, one sentence each.

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

• Practice A (6): solo + pairs; A3/A4 test the question/command pattern — force statement order aloud.

• Practice B (6): B1/B2 reported in pairs; B3/B4 corrections stated with the error.

• Key after checking; on any suggest-me-to-go error, re-teach Rule 3.

Answer key — Practice A and B (identical to the Student Book key)

Practice A. 1 was working · 2 had finished · 3 had parked (or: parked) · 4 not to · 5 to help · 6 taking

Practice B. 1 He said (that) he never lied. / He said (that) he never lies. · 2 They asked when the results would be announced. · 3 He told me that he was tired. · 4 She suggested going early. / She suggested that I go early. · 5 He denied breaking the window. · 6 answers vary

Where learners lose marks — teaching notes

• A1 'was working' — backshift from 'am working'; accept 'had been working' only if the learner explains the longer duration — do not mark as wrong automatically.

• A4 'not to' — warning/telling not to + base; 'not touch' bare would be wrong here.

• A6 'taking' — suggest + -ing; 'to take' is the flagged error (B4).

• B2 'would be announced' — will → would; do not accept 'will'.

• B5 denies the content, not the act: 'denied breaking the window' (deny + -ing).

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

• Message game: three 'other person' messages per A; B reports to a third listener.

• Four different reporting verbs + question + command required before stopping.

• Swap roles; whole class hears the clearest retelling chain.

Model exchange for rehearsal (one possible version)

A: My friend said she was worried about the interview. B: My friend said she was worried — she admitted she hadn't prepared enough. She said she would call me after, and her boss warned her not to arrive late. She asked me if I knew what questions would be asked. I suggested going to bed early and promised to send her my notes.

Part 6 · The Advanced Upgrade

• Intermediate base: backshift table drill + four chunk patterns.

• Advanced upgrade: 'kept insisting / went on to explain / points out / claimed…' — one true sentence per frame.

• Debate: when does 'He claimed' cast doubt vs just report?

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

• Planning: choose conversation, list four things said (who + keyword) + four verbs.

• 90 seconds to a partner; model covered.

• Model uncovered; count verbs, check backshift, compare with learners' own retelling and improve one sentence.

Model response (as printed in the Student Book)

On Saturday my sister called to tell me that she had accepted the job offer. She admitted that she was nervous, but she promised to ask for a training week. My father warned her not to sign without reading the contract, and she agreed to send it to him first. She also asked me whether I thought she should negotiate the salary; I suggested doing the same research she had done for the interview. In my opinion, she should ask — the worst they can say is no.

Assessing this open-ended task

• Count backshift, statement order, reporting-verb variety and time shift with the printed checks; accept a still-true present tense (L6 carryover) where justified.

• Accept any real conversation content; the model is not required copying.

• Prompt once for a missing question report if learners avoid it.

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

• Covered: report three things from today.

• Question/command/promise round — oral only.

• Self-check; unticked redo A1–A3 and B3 aloud.

Differentiation: Intermediate and Advanced pathways

Intermediate — scaffolding and remediation

• Board ladder stays visible; learners touch the step before speaking.

• Chunk desk card: 'admitted -ing · promised to · warned not to · suggested -ing'.

• Remediation: re-run say/tell and suggest fixes chorally before Real Talk.

Advanced — extension and discussion guidance

• Liveliness: 'She kept insisting…' vs 'She insisted…' — register?

• Academic stance: 'The report points out that demand has fallen' — learners build one.

• Judgement-free: 'He claimed to have seen nothing, yet…' — who is judged?

Common learner errors and targeted correction

Expect these — and fix them like this

• 'He said me…' → 'He told me…' — fix: say + that vs tell + person sort.

• 'She suggested me to go' → 'going' — fix: verb-pattern flash with four verbs.

• Keeping question inversion in reported form — fix: statement-order drill with two questions.

Shorter-session adaptation (45 minutes)

Keep the objective, cut the load

• Parts 1–4 at 15 + 10; message game runs two messages per role.

• Upgrade becomes homework sentences.

• Real Talk: 60 seconds with three reported items + comment.

Review, consolidation and feedback

Close the loop

• Exit ticket: report one question, one command, one promise from today.

• Reported speech is tested again in the Final Assessment (B1/B2) — flag those items.

• Formula card 13.

Feedback for this lesson's speaking

During pair reporting, tick reporting-verb count and backshift — do not correct mid-flow; rebuild two errors after the round, choosing the most frequent one first.

LESSON 14 · PARTICIPLES AND ADVANCED SENTENCE PATTERNS — TEACHER GUIDE

Part 7 — Sound More Natural and Advanced | Speaking goal: combine ideas concisely without losing clarity

This guide mirrors the Student Book lesson exactly: the same eight functions, the same practice items and the same answers. Follow the parts in order; adapt the timing to your class.

Lesson outcomes and measurable success criteria

By the end of the lesson

• Form participles and participle clauses accurately and keep the subject matching.

• Distinguish -ing (cause) from -ed (feeling) adjectives in speech.

• Open a formal recommendation with Given/Considering and a Having-clause.

Success criteria — the learner can:

✓ opening participle clauses match the subject of the main clause

✓ at least two accurate participle clauses per briefing

✓ -ed/-ing adjectives chosen correctly in description

Materials and preparation

Before the lesson

• Board: -ING = causes feeling · -ED = feels it (boring/bored).

• Frame strip: Given… / Considering… / With + noun + -ing / Having + participle.

• Formula Book card 14.

Suggested timing (60-minute lesson)

Lesson part

Minutes

The Speaking Hook

4

The Simple Rule

8

See the Difference

3

Practice the Pattern

10

Pair Speaking

12

The Advanced Upgrade

8

Real Talk Challenge

10

Review and Self-Check

5

Total

60

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

• Two-sentence combos: learners combine them any way they like — reveal how many chose a participle.

• Collect the most professional version whole-class; underline the participle.

• Name today's aim: compression without confusion.

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

• Rule 1: -ing vs -ed adjectives — choral drill of four pairs (boring/bored etc.).

• Rule 2: participle clauses — build one Having-example on the board step by step.

• Rule 3: absolute/fronted patterns — chorally read the three examples.

• Rule 4: compression with the learner-combine sentence: 'Opening the letter…'

Check understanding — quick, whole-class

• 'boring vs bored' — things are -ing, people are -ed; quick thumbs.

• 'Opening the window, the room was cold.' — correct? (no — who opened?) rebuild it.

• 'Given the costs, the plan is unrealistic' — who is giving? (frame, not verb)

Part 3 · See the Difference

• -ing vs -ed table: pairs state 'what causes? who feels?' for each row.

• Participle vs full clause table: same meaning comparison, emphasis on compression.

• Subject-rule warning: write the dangling example ('Opening the window, the room was cold') and repair it together.

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

• Practice A (6) solo + pairs; A3/A4 (Having…) need the participle type named aloud.

• Practice B (6): B1 spoken compressions in pairs; B3 as whole-class chorus.

• Key after checking; re-teach the subject rule if B3 was widely missed.

Answer key — Practice A and B (identical to the Student Book key)

Practice A. 1 boring · 2 amazed · 3 Having finished · 4 Having been warned / Warned · 5 With · 6 Walking

Practice B. 1 Having studied hard, she passed easily. · 2 The man standing at the door waved. · 3 Opening the window, I felt the cold air come in. / As I opened the window, the cold air came in. · 4 Given the costs, the plan is unrealistic. · 5 I am very interested in history. · 6 answers vary

Where learners lose marks — teaching notes

• A1 'boring' — lecture causes boredom; 'bored' would describe hearers.

• A5 'With' — absolute clause; 'Despite' would invert the meaning.

• B1 'Having studied hard…' — compresses 'Because…'; 'After' is also correct but less formal.

• B2 'The man standing at the door waved' — reduced correctly; 'The man who was standing' also credited.

• B5 'interested' — -ed = feels (about history); 'interesting' would make the person the cause.

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

• Formal briefing: each partner 60 seconds, two participle clauses, listener reports in one sentence.

• Monitor for Having-clause + Given/Considering + -ed/-ing pair.

• Swap; best briefing heard twice for the class.

Model exchange for rehearsal (one possible version)

A: Given the short deadline, we finished the work on time. Having worked late every evening, we were exhausted but satisfied. B: Was the client interested? A: Very — the proposal was fascinating, and the client was clearly impressed. With prices falling, they approved the plan quickly. B: So, having delivered early, are you now free? A: Considering the feedback, almost — just one report to go.

Part 6 · The Advanced Upgrade

• Intermediate base: -ed/-ing about real life + two correct openings from the week.

• Advanced upgrade: 'There being no…', 'Never having…', formal closings — one each.

• Discussion: 'Considering all the evidence, we recommend…' — who is considering?

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

• Planning: evidence → recommendation → closing — mark participle slots as printed.

• 90 seconds to a partner; model covered.

• Model uncovered; count clauses, compare subject matching, improve one learner sentence together.

Model response (as printed in the Student Book)

Given the number of late arrivals, we recommend shifting the morning meeting to nine o'clock. Having reviewed the attendance records, I noticed that most delays happen before ten, when the traffic is heaviest. The current schedule is frustrating for parents, and several tired employees arrive unprepared. Considering the cost of the change — none — the benefit is obvious. All things considered, a two-week trial would settle the question.

Assessing this open-ended task

• Assess the two printed checks plus subject matching — no dangling participle counts.

• Over-compression is penalised: require clarity alongside brevity.

• Model is one register choice; learners may choose a less formal briefing style if clauses are correct.

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

• Covered: 'Having…' sentence about today.

• One -ing and one -ed adjective about today — round-robin.

• Self-check; unticked redo B3 and A2 aloud.

Differentiation: Intermediate and Advanced pathways

Intermediate — scaffolding and remediation

• Subject-link arrow drawn between participle and main-clause subject during pair work.

• Frame card: 'Having finished…' · 'Given…' · 'With + noun…'

• Remediation: if B3 failed, rebuild one participle opening collaboratively before Real Talk.

Advanced — extension and discussion guidance

• Formality ladder: after/while/because → Having… / Walking… / Written in… — when formal?

• Story upgrade: 'Never having travelled abroad, he found…' — build one true.

• Formal closer: 'We recommend delaying the decision.'

Common learner errors and targeted correction

Expect these — and fix them like this

• 'Opening the window, the room was cold' (dangling) → '…I felt the cold' — fix: subject arrow drawn, then learner rebuild.

• 'I am very interesting in history' → 'interested' — fix: cause-vs-feel sorting.

• Over-participle speech ('Having… Having… Given…') — fix: one-two per answer is enough.

Shorter-session adaptation (45 minutes)

Keep the objective, cut the load

• Parts 1–4 at 15 + 10; briefing becomes 45 seconds with report-back.

• Advanced upgrade moves to a written homework example.

• Real Talk: keep both structures but deliver as 60 seconds.

Review, consolidation and feedback

Close the loop

• Exit ticket: one 'Having…' sentence + one absolute frame about today.

• Participles return in the Final Assessment (C10) — connect the revision.

• Formula card 14.

Feedback for this lesson's speaking

Tick participle openings and subject links during briefings — correct the first dangling participle the moment it is spoken (board repair), leave the second for the aftermath.

LESSON 15 · HEDGING, EMPHASIS, AND NATURAL INVERSION — TEACHER GUIDE

Part 8 — Speak with Confidence | Speaking goal: control certainty, emphasis and formality like an educated speaker

This guide mirrors the Student Book lesson exactly: the same eight functions, the same practice items and the same answers. Follow the parts in order; adapt the timing to your class.

Lesson outcomes and measurable success criteria

By the end of the lesson

• Hedge claims appropriately (may well / tend to / it could be argued).

• Apply cleft and inversion emphasis accurately and sparingly.

• Match certainty language to evidence in a formal talk.

Success criteria — the learner can:

✓ no inversion-error and no broken cleft in the pair and Real Talk

✓ at least one hedge placed per claim, never three in a row

✓ certainty level defensible by evidence when challenged

Materials and preparation

Before the lesson

• Board: will/must be (certain) · should/may well (likely) · may/might/could (possible).

• Frame cards: It is…that · What I…is · Never have I… · Not only did… Only then did…

• Formula Book card 15.

Suggested timing (60-minute lesson)

Lesson part

Minutes

The Speaking Hook

4

The Simple Rule

8

See the Difference

3

Practice the Pattern

10

Pair Speaking

12

The Advanced Upgrade

8

Real Talk Challenge

10

Review and Self-Check

5

Total

60

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

• Board 'The plan will fail' vs 'The plan may well fail' — class votes which sounds more educated, then defends with 'why?'

• Two learners say the same opinion: certain, then hedged — class names the difference.

• Aim: control of strength is control of credibility.

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

• Rule 1: hedging — read the three levels, then one example per frame.

• Rule 2: clefts — board-build 'It was the price that changed my mind' with focus marks.

• Rule 3: inversion — chorally read the three openers; underline the inverted aux.

• Rule 4: register ladder — same request in three registers, spoken by three learners.

Check understanding — quick, whole-class

• 'Never I have seen' — fix order. (have I)

• Three-level rapid: 'The plan will/may well/might succeed' — evidence for each?

• Cleft focus check: 'It was the manager who…' — what was focused? (the actor)

Part 3 · See the Difference

• Certainty table: pairs label will / may well / might with the three claims.

• Normal vs inversion table: normal on left, inverted on right — mark when inverted sounds heavy.

• Cleft table: same sentence, three spotlights — ask 'What is in focus?'

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

• Practice A (6) solo + pair; A1/A2/A3 test inversion form directly.

• Practice B (6): B1–B4 spoken transformations; B5 two-register performance aloud.

• Key after checking; drill 'Never have I…' chorally if A1 slipped.

Answer key — Practice A and B (identical to the Student Book key)

Practice A. 1 Never · 2 did she pass · 3 did I understand · 4 suggests (or: suggest) · 5 the deadline · 6 tends

Practice B. 1 This policy may well reduce costs. / This policy is likely to reduce costs. · 2 It was the price that changed my mind. · 3 Rarely had I felt so confident. · 4 Never have I seen such a mess. · 5 answers vary · 6 answers vary

Where learners lose marks — teaching notes

• A1 'Never' — negative-opener inversion; 'Ever' would not trigger it.

• A3 'did I understand' — 'Only after reading it twice' forces inversion.

• A4 flexible: both 'suggests' (data as collective) and 'suggest' (data as plural) credited, as stated in the key.

• B3 accepts 'Rarely had I felt so confident' or 'Rarely have I…' where the learner explains the past/future intention — past tense is the printed answer.

• B6 'Not only…but also' — the second clause's but/but also is optional in speech; credit either.

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

• Panel: 'What will work look like in ten years?' — one minute per partner + hard follow-up.

• Require hedge + cleft + conclusion in each answer.

• Follow-up answered carefully — monitor for hedging under pressure.

Model exchange for rehearsal (one possible version)

A: In ten years, remote work will be normal — it could be argued that offices will become meeting places only. B: It is flexibility that workers want most. A: Never have I been more confident that change is coming. B: Really — what evidence do you have? A: Studies suggest productivity rises 8%, and rarely have companies reported wanting to go back fully.

Part 6 · The Advanced Upgrade

• Intermediate base: three certainty groups in context + three inversion frames.

• Advanced upgrade: 'little did he know', litotes, conditional inversion — one each.

• Register check: 'This proposal may well…' vs 'It will…' — evidence matters?

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

• Planning as printed: claim+evidence → cleft focus → inversion → keywords only.

• Two minutes to a partner without notes; model covered.

• Model uncovered; count hedge/cleft/inversion, compare, improve one line.

Model response (as printed in the Student Book)

Education in my country will change in one area above all: access. It is broadband that will decide who benefits from that change. Rarely have we seen technology move so quickly in our cities, yet rural schools are often left without a reliable connection. The government could take the first step by funding internet in district centres — this may well be the cheapest investment of the decade. If the infrastructure were in place, teachers could share materials overnight. In closing, I would say one thing: connect the schools first, and the rest will follow.

Assessing this open-ended task

• Use the four feedback criteria as live ticks — hedging not over-hedging is the hardest to judge, so listen for stacked hedges.

• Inversion and cleft must be accurate; one correct example each is enough.

• Register must be consistently formal in Real Talk; one casual register slip is the limit before feedback.

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

• Covered: one claim at three certainty levels — rapid-fire.

• One cleft + one inversion from memory — round-robin.

• Self-check; unticked redo B4 and the paired certainty line aloud.

Differentiation: Intermediate and Advanced pathways

Intermediate — scaffolding and remediation

• Certainty desk card visible during all speaking.

• Frame prompts: 'This may well…' · 'It was X who…' · 'Never have I…'

• Remediation: if inversion slips, re-drill the three frames chorally before Real Talk.

Advanced — extension and discussion guidance

• Litotes: 'You are not wrong' vs 'You are right' — when softer?

• Formal conditional inversion: 'Were this accepted, we would…' — build one.

• Evidence check: challenge a learner's hedge — 'What evidence makes this may-well rather than might?'

Common learner errors and targeted correction

Expect these — and fix them like this

• 'Never I have seen' → 'Never have I…' — fix: negative opener → aux + subject order.

• Over-hedging ('It might perhaps possibly…') — fix: one careful hedge is enough; cross out two.

• Over-inverting every sentence — fix: once per talk for impact, marked with a star.

Shorter-session adaptation (45 minutes)

Keep the objective, cut the load

• Parts 1–4 at 15 + 10; panel runs one question per pair.

• Litotes/conditional-inversion become written homework.

• Real Talk: 90 seconds instead of two minutes — still three structures.

Review, consolidation and feedback

Close the loop

• Exit ticket: one cleft and one inversion about today.

• Hedging/Inversion return in Lessons 16 and the Final Assessment (rubric criterion 2/3).

• Formula card 15.

Feedback for this lesson's speaking

Name one well-judged hedge with its evidence — this teaches hedging better than generic praise; correct inversion order only in the repair phase.

LESSON 16 · GRAMMAR IN REAL CONVERSATION — TEACHER GUIDE

Part 8 — Speak with Confidence | Speaking goal: bring all the course grammar together in free, accurate, confident speech

This guide mirrors the Student Book lesson exactly: the same eight functions, the same practice items and the same answers. Follow the parts in order; adapt the timing to your class.

Lesson outcomes and measurable success criteria

By the end of the lesson

• Integrate time, choice, shape and style grammar in continuous speech.

• Self-repair accurately and keep speaking without freezing.

• Prepare for the Final Assessment speaking task conditions.

Success criteria — the learner can:

✓ at least six different target structures used in the two-minute talk

✓ at least one self-repair performed aloud with a repair phrase

✓ story shape (background → decision → goal) clear to the listener

Materials and preparation

Before the lesson

• Four-job map printed: TIME · CHOICE · SHAPE · STYLE — visible to every pair.

• Repair phrases on desk card: 'What I mean is…' · 'Let me rephrase…' · 'Or rather…'

• Timer set to 2 minutes; Final Assessment rubric to hand.

Suggested timing (60-minute lesson)

Lesson part

Minutes

The Speaking Hook

4

The Simple Rule

7

See the Difference

4

Practice the Pattern

10

Pair Speaking

13

The Advanced Upgrade

7

Real Talk Challenge

10

Review and Self-Check

5

Total

60

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

• 30-second topic to a partner; listeners name every structure they recognise.

• Two learners' lists on the board — which four-job bucket is missing?

• Aim: today nothing is new — today nothing is hidden either.

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

• Four-job map: place every course structure in one bucket together — learners touch each item on their copy.

• Three-step strategy: THINK meaning → CHOOSE structure → SAY it whole — rehearse with one repair example aloud.

• Remind: accuracy before range, every time.

Check understanding — quick, whole-class

• Four-job map rapid: 'passive?' (shape) — 'wish?' (choice) — 'hedging?' (style)

• Repair challenge: give a wrong-sentence starter — learners repair aloud.

• Six-structure sprint: count structures heard in 30 seconds.

Part 3 · See the Difference

• Recognition vs use — ask 'Which is harder?' — expect: producing under pressure.

• Ask pairs to list one structure per job from their own life in 60 seconds.

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

• Practice A (6) fix-and-explain: each error named and corrected aloud — no silent marking.

• Practice B (6): B1 participle spoken; B2–B6 spoken in pairs with brief discussion.

• Key after pair checking; use B2 as the reported-speech recap point.

Answer key — Practice A and B (identical to the Student Book key)

Practice A. 1 I saw him yesterday. (finished time) · 2 If I have time, I will help. · 3 Despite the price, we bought it. / Although it was expensive, we bought it. · 4 He suggested waiting. / He suggested that I wait. · 5 Never have I been so tired. · 6 I look forward to meeting you.

Practice B. 1 Not having slept, he made errors. · 2 She told me not to worry. / She reassured me. · 3 answers vary — degree word + reason required · 4 The schedule has been changed. · 5 This method may well be the best. / This method is probably the best. (answers vary) · 6 answers vary — indirect word order required

Where learners lose marks — teaching notes

• A1–A6 are fix-and-explain — insist on the explanation, not just the correction; these are course retrospection items.

• B2 'She told me not to worry / She reassured me' — both credited; reassured is not a reporting verb but a semantic equivalent here.

• B6 requires indirect (word order) — any polite indirect question on tomorrow's schedule is open.

• B5 accepts any well-formed hedge; B3 accepts any degree-word + reason comparison.

• Practice workload here is intentionally integrated — A/B together revise 12 structures.

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

• Grammar gym: four rounds, one minute per round (storytelling/advice/report/argument).

• Partner counts target structures per round and reports one strength.

• Best round per pair replayed for the class as the exemplar.

Model exchange for rehearsal (one possible version)

A: Last year I almost quit English when I failed the first exam — I was working nights and had little time. B: How did you continue? A: A friend told me to focus on speaking, not translation. If I had stopped, I would have lost the chance — as it was, I passed. B: So what is your argument for the school? A: If the school funds evening speaking clubs, students will improve faster — a small cost, a clear result. To sum up, start with the learners who need it most.

Part 6 · The Advanced Upgrade

• Intermediate base: re-do the hardest earlier exercise aloud; three sentences per job.

• Advanced upgrade: stacked 'Had I known…' sentence, style opening, repair phrases — one each performed.

• Discussion: when does a repair show control vs when it hides it?

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

• Planning exactly as printed: three lines (story / decision / goal) + two 'show-off' structures chosen deliberately.

• Two minutes to a partner without notes; model covered.

• Model uncovered; count structures, compare story shape to the printed feedback, improve one line, then repeat once to a new partner.

Model response (as printed in the Student Book)

Two years ago I avoided speaking English in class because I was afraid of mistakes — I would translate every sentence in my head first. Joining a speaking club changed that: within a month, I had made friends who corrected me kindly. Since then I have been practising almost every day, and my teachers have noticed the difference. I've decided to take the TOEFL next spring, which is why I'm recording myself twice a week. If I keep this up, the score will take care of itself. What I need most now is confidence under pressure — and that comes only from speaking.

Assessing this open-ended task

• Count structures heard against the printed four criteria; repairs are scored as a positive, not a penalty.

• This lesson is also the Final Assessment speaking rehearsal — score with the same rubric and keep the scores.

• Accept any topic that shows range; the model is one path, not the required content.

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

• Covered: name the four jobs + one structure per job.

• One-minute story with three structures — volunteer.

• Self-check; unticked means re-open the Formula Book, not the next book.

Differentiation: Intermediate and Advanced pathways

Intermediate — scaffolding and remediation

• Four-job map always visible; learners point to the job before choosing the structure.

• Repair phrase desk card stays out for every round.

• Remediation: learners who froze re-do the three-line plan before the next attempt.

Advanced — extension and discussion guidance

• Stacking: 'Had I known…' as the show-off structure — pairs judge clarity vs complexity.

• Style intention: open with inversion, hedge the claim, close with a cleft — deliberate style, not decoration.

• Repair sophistication: 'Or rather…' vs 'What I mean is…' — when more formal?

Common learner errors and targeted correction

Expect these — and fix them like this

• Complexity before accuracy — fix: 'Simple and correct beats fancy and wrong' on the board.

• Freezing on an error — fix: repair phrase drill (five errors rebuilt with 'What I mean is').

• Stacking too many structures in one sentence until it collapses — fix: one hard structure per sentence, maximum.

Shorter-session adaptation (45 minutes)

Keep the objective, cut the load

• Parts 1–4 at 15 + 10; grammar gym runs two rounds chosen by teacher.

• Two remaining gym rounds become the take-home spoken homework (recorded).

• Real Talk: still two minutes — do not shorten Lesson 16's culminating talk.

Review, consolidation and feedback

Close the loop

• Exit ticket: one story with three structures, spoken — recorded if possible.

• Next class is the Final Assessment — use today's rubric scores as the true baseline companion to the Diagnostic.

• Formula cards: entire book. The Can-Do Tracker (Student Book Appendix 4) is today's takeaway.

Feedback for this lesson's speaking

Celebrate self-repairs as evidence of control — announce the repair phrase you heard; correct only the single most repeated structural error for the class, after every round.

ASSESSMENT GUIDANCE

Keys, alternatives, speaking tasks and score honesty

Where the answers live

• Lesson practice answers: printed inside every guide (identical to Student Book Appendix 5).

• Diagnostic Test, Review Tests 1–3 and Final Assessment keys: printed in the back matter of this book; learners see them only in Student Book Appendix 5, after they have worked.

• Open-ended speaking tasks: never keyed to a single response. Use the success criteria in each task and the four-criterion rubric (Grammatical accuracy · Appropriate structure selection · Clarity · Successful communication; 1–4 each, total 16).

Marking rules

• Accept every alternative the key marks as acceptable; multiple defensible answers are acknowledged in the key, not penalised.

• Where an item admits several readings and the key does not acknowledge them, treat it as a discussion item — do not invent a single mandatory answer.

• For transformations, credit any version that preserves the target structure and meaning.

• Record speaking scores by criterion, not as one global impression, and keep the baseline and final rubric scores side by side.

• Do not compare Diagnostic and Final raw grammar totals as a measure of gain — the tests differ in length and blueprint. Compare rubric criterion scores instead.

Model final speaking response (one strong example, not a script)

Approximately two minutes, delivered without reading

A decision that changed my life was moving to Kabul for university.
At first I had never lived away from my family, and I was not sure I could manage alone. While I was adjusting, I made mistakes — I spent too much on transport because I had not learned the bus routes. If I had known the city better, I would have saved both time and money, and I would be more relaxed now. I believe education is an investment, although it was hard to leave home. I was told that grades would depend on attendance, so I attended every class. I have enjoyed meeting people who come from other provinces; the diversity has taught me patience. I have decided to continue studying even though costs are high. What I hope to do next is pass the TOEFL and teach English — the course has shown me that speaking every day is the key. Never have I been more certain that effort, not talent, decides who improves.

Score it with the printed rubric: note the criterion scores, then discuss with the speaker which one or two behaviours would move a 3 to a 4. Learner responses that differ in content but meet the criteria must score the same as the model.

Keys — Diagnostic Test and Review Tests

Diagnostic

A. 1 saw · 2 has worked / has been working · 3 was cooking · 4 had worked / had been working; 'worked' is also possible with before · 5 boils · 6 were building · 7 have lost · 8 went · 9 have read · 10 had already left

B. 1 rains · 2 knew · 3 repairing / to be repaired · 4 was written · 5 leaving · 6 the station is · 7 who / that · 8 didn't smoke · 9 more intelligent · 10 did she finish

C. 1 can't · 2 Despite · 3 where I lived / where I live (if still true) · 4 may / might / could · 5 had / got

Review Test 1

A. 1 haven't seen · 2 were waiting · 3 freezes · 4 is studying · 5 had eaten · 6 is going to rain / will rain · 7 have / known · 8 started

B. 1 must · 2 Would / closing · 3 is · 4 don't have to / needn't

C. 1 Answers vary; e.g., 'You should rest before driving.' (should + base verb) · 2 Could you tell me where you parked? · 3 must be

Review Test 2

A. 1 knew · 2 had taken · 3 more effective · 4 was reading · 5 had already left · 6 made · 7 best · 8 hurry

B. 1 Despite the exam being hard, everyone passed. / Despite the difficulty, everyone passed. · 2 If I had a car, I would drive you. / If I had a car, I could drive you. · 3 answers vary — advice with should/could/might · 4 Could you tell me where the bank is?

C. 1 If she had saved money, she could buy the car now. / …would be able to buy… · 2 answers vary — far + comparative + reason · 3 Despite the cost, we decided to proceed.

Review Test 3

A. 1 was built · 2 repaired · 3 to speak · 4 making · 5 where · 6 whose · 7 didn't mention · 8 knew

B. 1 The room needs cleaning. / The room needs to be cleaned. · 2 He must have missed the train. · 3 Students interested in the course should apply. · 4 It is believed that the economy is improving. / The economy is believed to be improving.

C. 1 more / more confident · 2 Do you know where the bank is? · 3 had · 4 I enjoy reading novels.

Key — Final Assessment (30 items)

A. 1 have lived / 've lived / have been living · 2 had already had · 3 is · 4 hadn't said · 5 was cancelled · 6 must have been working · 7 making · 8 rewrite · 9 challenging · 10 Warned / Having been warned · 11 leaving · 12 did she apologise

B. 1 He said he would help me the next day. · 2 She asked me where I had bought it. · 3 Could you tell me when the shop closes? · 4 If he had revised, he wouldn't have failed. · 5 The documents have been stolen. · 6 It was the manager who/that approved the plan. · 7 I had the roof fixed. · 8 Rarely had she felt so confident. · 9 Although the task was difficult, they finished it. · 10 Having studied hard, he passed easily.

C. 1 can't · 2 Despite · 3 This method may well be the best. / This method is probably the best. (answers vary) · 4 Option A is far better than Option B because… (answers vary) · 5 The book (that / which) I read was amazing. · 6 more confident · 7 She advised me to apply early. · 8 meeting

Answer notes for the tests

• Review Test 1 A4 'is studying': 'these days' frames a temporary current situation; past simple here would contradict the time cue.

• Review Test 1 B1 'must': legal obligation; B4 'don't have to / needn't': absence of obligation — not 'mustn't', which would mean prohibition.

• Review Test 2 B1: accept both 'Despite the exam being hard, everyone passed' and 'Despite the difficulty, everyone passed' — the first keeps the -ing complement attached to the exam, not to everyone.

• Review Test 3 A3: 'is said to speak' — reporting structure from Lesson 9; keep the infinitive, not a finite tense.

• Final Assessment A1 accepts 'have lived / 've lived / have been living' — all three describe a situation continuing to now with 'since 2020'.

• Final Assessment C3 accepts 'may well / probably / is likely to' and any equivalent well-formed hedge; C4 is credited with any far/much/a lot + comparative + reason frame.

• Diagnostic items accept the alternatives listed in the key (for example 'has worked / has been working', 'who / that', 'may / might / could', 'had / got').
